Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through clustering of projection points or correspondence of virtual control points. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining projection clustering and correspondence of virtual control points to estimate 6D poses. We integrated projection clustering to filter out unreliable predictions and correspondence of virtual control points to enhance pose accuracy without increasing the number of model parameters. Object poses estimated through our method ranked first in the BOP-2019 Challenge. We also tested our model on the LINEMOD dataset and found a 12.3% reduction in the average distance between predicted and ground truth poses. All experiments were conducted utilizing the DeepHMap++ dataset, which we hope will be beneficial for future research. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/lingyu-92/DeepHMap++.oral.

In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. Our findings reveal that increased intermediate speeds shorten pinch-off times, and other factors like surface tension and vibration in spheres also affect pinch-off times. By analyzing these findings within the context of other water-entry problems, such as buoyancy-induced vibration, our research provides a more comprehensive understanding of the surface seal regime. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a quicker and more efficient approach using alone CT scans for accurately identifying tumors in the esophagus. A novel deep learning model called Dense Focus Unet (DFUnet) is introduced, which produces detailed mappings from basic features, and a modified version called Dense Focus Average Unet (DDAUnet) that produces less detailed mappings is proposed. By combining the output of these models, DDAUnet demonstrates superior performance in mapping precision and average score for esophageal tumor segmentation on two separate datasets. The model's effectiveness is further validated through a simple airway mask-based approach that simplifies the segmentation process by removing the upper part of the esophagus, resulting in an overall score improvement of 12.5% in the public dataset and 21.5% in the hospital dataset. The model's efficiency in annotating unseen CT scans as well as its robustness in treating protruding external objects was also demonstrated. Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is crucial, and one widely used method is comparing them to human-generated captions. Although, as some researchers have pointed out, relying solely on human benchmarks without consideration for their creation mechanisms may lead to misinterpretation of results. Human benchmarks are often constructed through large-scale data mining without considering how descriptions are actually created. If descriptions referencing the same object use different words, such as "cat" versus "feline", or "dog" versus "canine", it can be difficult to measure description quality. On the other hand, human descriptions do reflect how descriptions can be created using existing resources, as they often incorporate a wide range of labels and synonyms. In a novel approach, we analyzed the frequency and creation rules of human descriptions to develop a method for evaluating descriptions that take into account the level of label overlap required. To demonstrate this method's utility, we created an automated system that generates descriptions with rules similar to those observed in the human dataset, and compared it to a widely used baseline. The results show that our evaluation method reveals aspects of description quality that are blind to label frequency, such as the system's tendency to use complex descriptions referred to as "compound phrases". The research also highlights opportunities for improving description generation, by analyzing common errors like the system's difficulty in using synonyms or combining the labels for different objects within the same image. The evaluation method presented here is specific to the MS COCO dataset, but its potential applications are vast, offering a framework that can be adapted to other image description datasets. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/TextGyu/evaluation-of-image-description. The findings are further illustrated with a sample system output shown in Figure 1, and the evaluation method's components are summarized in Table 1. The research into human benchmark datasets is ongoing, and we are exploring the opportunities presented by the approach developed, such as the detection of label overlap requirements for existing datasets like the VGG Sound Net, for the image-region annotation datasets like the CVC-12, and for the description datasets that incorporate attribute information like the Attribute Captioning Dataset. The approach presented here is unique in comparing the distribution of human descriptions with the quality of automatic descriptions, and it offers a novel perspective on the evaluation of image description generation systems. The method's potential applications extend beyond the evaluation of image description generation systems, as it can also detect the overlap required for other tasks such as the generation of natural language statements referring to images. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing system for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This paper also introduces a novel approach to comparing utterances that takes into account their semantic content, as well as a simple strategy for evaluating system behavior. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality assurance processes, including machine learning-based methods that utilize limited training data. This study involves evaluating various generalization strategies for MRI quality assessment, focusing on projections that reduce data dimensions and representations that distill information from sensitive attributes, such as background severity. We investigated multiple techniques, analyzing their individual components and combined effects to enhance model performance. Our research utilizes a subset of publicly available MRI data, specifically the iMRI brain data. Our findings show that combining low-dimensional projections with attention-based mechanisms and using random forest as our base model leads to the best results, with an F-score of 87% in predicting low-quality images. Nevertheless, this study highlights the significance of further customization, given that the highest average F-score among reference methods is only 3% higher than the most basic approach. Moreover, larger-scale MRI datasets are required to thoroughly explore generalization strategies, as well as large-scale brain segmentation and synthesis datasets, to further innovate in the field of MRI quality assessment. The code and data for this research are available at https://github.com/ghassab/BrainMRI-QA.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of distribution networks, we developed a decision-making framework for optimal charging and driving paths utilizing a mix of short-term and long-term objectives. A two-layer optimization approach was implemented, featuring a dual-layer structure where micro-level decisions on charging and driving are made individually by vehicle owners, and these individual choices contribute to a collective impact that affects the overall stability of the distribution network. A computational study was conducted to evaluate the effects of various factors including network configuration, and it showed that private electric vehicles can contribute positively to the efficiency and sustainability of distribution networks, but may also pose risks to network stability and continuity. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of considering non-utility-based short-term behaviors and long-term customs crucial to the assessment and management of distribution network resilience. A critical finding also emerged that a network's resilience can be improved through suitable pricing policies and targeted promotions of specific driving and charging habits. Full-scale implementation of private electric vehicles also raises important considerations about data availability, modeling challenges, and novel indicators of network resilience, and these issues are addressed in the study. Our research can be applied to similar decision-making problems involving complex, interconnected systems and can be extended to other contexts such as micro-grids and smart transportation systems. Our optimization framework, together with the underlying methodology and performance results, are available upon request to interested parties. The data used for the analysis and the code are available online at https://github.com/JiangJiang100/simulation. Unlike traditional approaches, this method disregards the focus on dialogue alone and instead, generates meetings through the convergence of individual drives, taking into consideration the unique characteristics and internal processes of each participating agent. Utilizing generative adversarial training and a distinct design for encouraging diversity, a notable aspect of this framework is a motor controller made available for free, which can be employed for various conversations and meetings. Alongside multi-agent encounters, it also enables individual characters to engage in monologues. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we evaluated the electronic and magnetic properties of the (100) and (111) surface layers for the materials. Lastly, potential phase transitions and surface magnetic moments exist for the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, which deserve further investigation.

We examine the concentration of random variables involving pairwise anti-correlated Bernoulli random variables and provide new inequalities to capture their deviation from their expected value. For a set of $n$ variables with a correlation structure defined by a graph represented as an undirected tree, we derive specific concentration inequalities that account for the tree's properties, such as its length, maximum degree, and minimum number of edges per node. These inequalities can be applied to a single variable or provide a total variation norm bound for the discrepancy of the distribution of the sum of these variables from a uniform distribution. Additionally, we demonstrate the relevance of these inequalities to systematic sampling and Gaussian random graphs. Furthermore, our results can be viewed as a modification of previous inequalities for independent random variables, offering an improved bound that incorporates the effect of mutual correlation. Lastly, our approach also yields an approximate maximum of the total variation norm, which may be of independent interest. For the case of a regular tree of depth $d$ and degree $\Delta$, with $\Delta \geq 2$, we obtain specific bounds, such as $n^{d/4}$ for the total variation norm of the sum's distribution and $n^{d/2}$ for the bound on the largest variable. These results extend previously known bounds for an independent random vector defined on the same tree. Our approach is largely based on a variation of the famous "double tree" reconstruction algorithm that is used to explore the structure of a distribution and its associated tree, as well as on a technique called the "relative log-Sobolev inequality". It also involves a graph theory component that involves the original correlation graph. Which enables us to derive an upper bound on the maximum variable, as well as on the total variation norm of the distribution of the sum of the random variables. A key challenge in modern organ transplantation involves managing kidney donations. Some patients registered for kidney transplants have existing matches, but others do not. On the other hand, some donated kidneys cannot be matched to any patient. A natural desire arises to prioritize those patients who already have a match, in order to increase the chances of a successful transplant. However, limiting transplantation to matched patient-kidney pairs also results in wasted potential kidney donations. To address this dilemma, a mathematical model is needed that can optimize organ allocation. In the context of kidney transplants, researchers use the concept of a "exchange algorithm." These algorithms allow two patient-kidney pairs to exchange kidneys if one donor is compatible with the recipient of the other pair. By extending exchange algorithms to involve three or more pairs, it's possible to increase the number of transplants performed. In a recent study, researchers implemented such an algorithm in the United States and Canada, resulting in a significant increase in successful transplants. Although prior studies mainly focused on static models, a new approach involves using dynamic models to track patient-kidney pair arrivals and departures over time. By incorporating priority given to patients with existing matches, this model can provide insights into how temporary increases in donated kidneys or patients registered for transplants impact the number of transplants performed in the short and long term. Furthermore, this model can also determine the optimal number of patient-kidney pairs to prioritize in different scenarios. In a real-world application, this model was used to analyze the kidney transplant program in Ontario, Canada, yielding predictions on how changes in program policies could affect transplant performance over time. This model has significant implications for other kidney transplant programs looking to improve transplant efficiency. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. In multiagent systems, an equilibrium is a stable state where agents' actions do not change, reflecting a balance of interests and potential countermeasures. However, the complexity of the underlying system often renders equilibria difficult to understand and analyze for individual agents or external observers. In our research, we develop a general framework for the first time that can recover an explainable representation of the equilibria in multiagent systems, even for large-scale systems where data is collected anonymously. We show that our approach can be applied to a range of models, including noncooperative games, evolutionary dynamics, and learning models, and demonstrates practical utility on real-world data, including an open dataset from online auctions. We believe this work paves the way for a deeper understanding of complex multiagent systems and the development of strategies for rewarding transparency. Our research is available online.

An analysis of a stochastic epidemic model is performed, where a changing network is modeled using a continuous-time random walk with preventive rewiring. The model involves an undirected graph whose edges change at unknown rates, and the epidemic spreads at a rate proportional to the product of the densities of infected individuals in the population and the number of infected neighbors for each edge. The aim is to determine the spread rate of the epidemic, which is found to be equal to the average time it takes for an edge to become connected to an infected individual, divided by the average time an edge spends connected to an infected individual before being reconnected to a healthy individual. The results include the expression of the epidemic's duration as a product of the rates associated with the edges and the initial number of infected individuals, and the fact that the epidemic always results in the destruction of the most connected edges in the graph. The study also provides an approximate solution for a specific type of network, and the expression for the epidemic's duration in the case where the rates associated with the edges are very fast. The research ends by discussing the implications of the model for the study of complex networks and the efficacy of the random walk model used. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source version of the Wikipedia infrastructure, enabling groups to create private knowledge bases for collaborative research, development, and project management. Originally developed in 2003 by Wikimedia Foundation's precursor, WorkingWiki has seen several iterations, currently utilizing PHP's Symfony framework and MariaDB database management system. This document outlines WorkingWiki's distinct features, contrasting them with Wikipedia, and provides an overview of its technical components, in addition to discussing potential applications and related projects. Although WorkingWiki shares a similar appearance with Wikipedia, its primary focus is on managing and organizing content, rather than editing articles for public consumption. One notable difference is the absence of automated editing tools on WorkingWiki, making it more suitable for reviewing and validating contributions. With an emphasis on collaborative work, WorkingWiki offers tools for task management, to-do lists, and project planning, making it appealing to diverse audiences, including business teams, academic groups, and non-profit organizations. This document is intended to guide developers in setting up a custom WorkingWiki instance, in addition to providing an overview of the platform's capabilities for potential users. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in reactions that occur within the flame and how they influence the flame's shape and position. By applying this approach in a linear framework, we were able to assess the reaction's stability and the flame's response to different frequencies of vibration. Our results show that the framework effectively replicates the reaction's behavior and could be used to determine places where flames are likely to become unstable in jet flames experiencing turbulence. Furthermore, we found that the $ka$ value, which indicates stability based on the wavenumber $k$ and the flame's length $a$, is a precise measure of a flame's response to vibration. Our research also reveals that the response of a flame to vibration is influenced primarily by the vibration's frequency and its own length, rather than the flow's turbulence. Lastly, we discovered that the model's accuracy could be improved by taking into account the vibration's impact on the flow's temperature and how this affects the flame's position. Lastly, we propose a simpler method for calculating the response of a flame to vibration, based on the time it takes for a flame to move a distance equal to its own length. Our investigation combines newly available functional genomic data and updated genome-wide association studies to analyze 18 human traits, with results that shed light on the underlying mechanisms of several traits, including inflammation-related genetics, immune system disorders, hemorrhagic stroke, prostate cancer, obesity, and certain psychiatric conditions. For the majority of traits, only a small fraction of associated genomic elements had known functions, highlighting the need for further research to uncover the functional aspects of many genomic elements. Our study reveals that genomic elements with regulatory capabilities, such as transcription factors, play a limited role in associating with traits, whereas protein-coding regions, mutations, and epigenetic elements contribute more significantly to associations with traits. By integrating genome-wide association studies with functional annotations, we found that only a small portion of associated genomic elements, around 1-5%, could be explained by existing biological knowledge. Thermodynamics and phonon scattering can significantly impact the behavior of electrons, affecting their motion, position, and orbital occupation in solids. Despite their crucial role, the limited resolution of phonon momentum measurement capabilities has hindered a quantitative understanding of these interactions. A new theoretical model aims to address this limitation by providing a comprehensive analysis of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions across all momentum modes available in solids. This model serves as a universal framework that can be applied to any solid, facilitating the calculation of interaction strengths and scattering probabilities for all momentum components of phonons. As a result, this approach makes it possible to identify the key phonon modes responsible for particular effects, even in complex and large-scale systems. To illustrate the model's utility, it is applied to titanium dioxide, revealing that the band splitting caused by phonon scattering is oriented perpendicular to the local ferromagnetic moment direction and that the associated wavevectors are directly linked to the underlying crystal structure. Furthermore, this model highlights the unique effects of momentum-dependent interactions, such as the resonance of electron states, the formation of energy bands caused by phonon fluctuations, and the influence of phonon motion on electron spin and orbital occupation. By comparing calculation results with available experimental data, it is shown that the resonance of electron states at specific wavevectors can resonate at particular lattice displacement components, thereby influencing the phonon frequency and spectral weight, and that the resulting change in frequency can be quite substantial, amounting to over 20%. Consequently, this model demonstrates that the resolution of phonon momentum measurement capabilities is insufficient for correctly interpreting the dynamics of phonon motion and scattering on the time-scale of lattice vibrations, which can influence the behavior of electrons in solids. Ultimately, this framework's versatility makes it suitable for integrating with a range of theoretical and experimental approaches, including phonon spectroscopies, density functional theory, dynamical mean-field theory, and time-resolved experiments. Understanding the meaning of conversations relies on grasping the semantics of individual turns and combining them to capture the overall meaning of the dialogue. In this paper, we explore the connection between dialogue semantics and Natural Language Inference (NLI). We introduce a novel NLI task called Dialogue Inference, where the hypothesis represents a subsequent dialogue turn, and the premise a previous turn. We also create a large-scale dataset, DoCoNLP, comprising 20,000 annotated NLP tasks that feature dialogue turns. Our findings reveal that models pre-trained on DoCoNLP outperform those pre-trained on general NLI datasets when evaluating dialogue semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NLI models pre-trained on DoCoNLP accurately distinguish between correct and incorrect continuations of a given dialogue. Our research takes the innovative step of incorporating NLI within the context of dialogue, offering a wealth of information on the complex topic of dialogue semantics. Our codes and datasets are available at github.com/ThuNLP/DoCoNLP. For future development, we propose two avenues: integrating BART-based models and exploring other NLP tasks that can be applied to dialogue. Moreover, we outline five future research questions in this domain. Lastly, we make our data collection framework publicly available, encouraging the incorporation of additional NLP tasks that can further enrich DoCoNLP. Our research in dialogue semantics is influenced by the groundbreaking work of Holtzman et al. and the acclaimed paper by Dodge and Gurtubay. The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
artificial neural networks. Although widely adopted in other contexts, these methods 
have not been heavily employed for amplitude analyses. The article also introduces 
new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density 
estimation utilizing artificial neural networks.  The aim of this article is to encourage
other researchers to employ these models in their own amplitude analysis studies. 
The article's content is accessible to those without a machine learning background.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. Unlike the conventional afterglow model, this novel approach takes into account various factors such as the energy conservation, both before and after the afterglow becomes non-relativistic, and it shows that afterglow dynamics can be understood through a simple, second-order equation. This model has been applied to a specific scenario involving an observed X-ray and optical afterglow, and it yields reliable predictions that are consistent with observed data. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that this model can accurately describe the transition from the initial, observed phases of afterglows, which typically follow a non-relativistic geometry, even in cases where the observed afterglow undergoes a transition from non-relativistic to relativistic phase. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative procedure for discovering such a representation and includes an analysis of its performance characteristics. Specifically, it proves that the method can handle instances where the number of nodes exceeds a limit that is directly proportional to the number of edges, combined with a factor accounting for the complexity of the representation's structure. The paper also explores the method's applicability to two-related problems: generating random 2D layouts and creating circle drawings, proposing a new metric to evaluate the former problem's hardness. The approach has been implemented and made available as an open-source tool, demonstrating its effectiveness on real-world data sets compared to existing methods. The paper's results have been presented at the symposium, along with a performance award for its peer-reviewed application to a practical problem. The research has further been distinguished with an honorary award. Total domains are then characterized by their integration theory, specifically through the totality of their valued field. This property is also shown to be equivalent to the integrality domain's having a specific property called strong stability. Within the framework of equicharacteristic extensions, a domain's total nature is found to be stable under extension, although it's not a hereditary property. Additionally, we provide examples of total domains, including some with a specific property called superconductivity, as well as those whose valued fields are not global. In order to make efficient use of power consumption and heat generation in large-scale cloud computing environments, a new approach is proposed that involves decreasing CPU frequencies across all cores by a certain percentage. A simulation was conducted on an actual data center dataset consisting of 200 workloads and spanning various CPU frequencies, and the results showed that reducing frequencies by as little as 20% across all cores can lead to a 10% decrease in overall energy consumption. Furthermore, a comparison was drawn with existing temperature reduction techniques, and the results indicated that decreasing CPU frequencies by a small percentage can also result in a significant decrease in average temperature, which in turn can lead to a 23.2% decrease in processor failure rate. A novel metric called the Energy Temperature Degradation Ratio (ETDR) was introduced to evaluate this kind of frequency-based degradation, and simulation results showed that it varies greatly depending on the data center environment, temperature requirements, and available processing power. Ultimately, the most suitable frequency reduction percentage was determined to be around 30% based on the ETDR calculations, and this kind of degradation was found to be a cost-effective measure that can result in significant energy savings and decreased maintenance costs in cloud computing environments. The proposed technique and the ETDR metric also have applications in fields beyond cloud computing. The simulation code has been made available online for further research and experimentation. This paper delves into the realm of federated learning, particularly in a vertical cross-domain setting, where entities with distinct data datasets collaborate to train a joint model. We highlight two privacy-exploiting attacks, which we refer to as privacy assaults, that target a bank and a mobile phone operator collaborating to train a model for fraud detection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks, along with a statistical analysis of their implications. A statistical examination of the underlying data distributions is a critical factor in executing these attacks, as we demonstrate these exploits to be precise to the degree of accuracy in these distributions. Furthermore, we contend that these attacks can be carried out by any individual with a superficial understanding of mathematics and statistics, without the need for extensive technical expertise. Our research into privacy assaults on the bank and the mobile phone operator reveals that the attacks' success is a direct consequence of the inherent flaws in the federated learning protocol itself. We have obtained two primary results regarding these hypersurfaces. Measurements of neutrino oscillation lengths primarily rely on accurate knowledge of the distance from the Sun to the neutrino source, a concern for long-period neutrino variations originating within the Sun. Previous research suggested a possible neutrino oscillation effect on solar neutrino data, specifically affecting the $^8$B neutrino flux. We evaluated the influence of neutrino oscillation lengths on solar neutrino data, particularly $^8$B and $^7$Be neutrino fluxes, using neutrino oscillation parameters recently established through experiments with artificial neutrino beams. We found that even the most significant uncertainty in the $^8$B neutrino flux reduction could be as small as 3.5%, and that neutrino oscillation lengths are unlikely to significantly impact the beam neutrino fluxes used in nuclear physics and astrophysical experiments beyond the current level of precision. Additionally, we propose a term, "Big Apple strength," to describe the electric field within the solar core and have calculated its possible ranges and the associated effects on the $^8$B and $^7$Be neutrino fluxes. We also explored the relationship between the Big Apple strength and the characteristics of finite nuclei, as well as its impact on astrophysical objects, particularly relativistic stars and rotating neutron stars. We found that the Big Apple strength is directly related to the nuclear density and the underlying shell effects, which influence the electron capture rates in finite nuclei. We also discovered that the Big Apple strength has a limited effect on the characteristics of finite nuclei and the behavior of rotating neutron stars, which can be safely neglected given the level of precision in current measurements. However, we found that the Big Apple strength could be significant for certain isolated neutron stars, specifically those with extremely low rates of rotation. We propose that the Big Apple strength offers a novel perspective on the interconnection between nuclear physics, solar neutrino physics, and the behavior of rotating neutron stars, and that it provides a meaningful approach to investigating the properties of finite nuclei and the characteristics of neutron stars through the study of solar neutrino data. We also discovered that the Big Apple strength is directly related to the oscillation length of neutrinos within the Sun, which influences the neutrino fluxes and offers a novel explanation for the long-period variations in the $^8$B neutrino flux. We propose that the Big Apple strength can be further investigated through a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental measurements, specifically through the analysis of long-period variations in the $^8$B neutrino flux

This research focuses on creating precise, long-lasting Molmer-Sorensen gates using multiple motional modes in an optical dipole trap for trapped ions. Initially, a theoretical framework is established to demonstrate how frequency-stable gates can be achieved when multiple motional modes contribute equally. Unlike traditional Molmer-Sorensen gates, the coherence remains resistant to fluctuations caused by certain motional mode couplings, thereby significantly increasing the stability of the gate. Furthermore, calculations indicate that despite the use of a 100-fold background fluctuation due to a specific motional mode, the gate's coherence can still be maintained for over 10 seconds, primarily as a result of the mode's minor contribution to the total motion. In practice, frequency stabilization of the gates is achieved by shaping the beam profile of the trap, which in the example given is shown to successfully deploy a specific combination of 3 motional modes, resulting in a W-state gate duration of approximately 1.8 milliseconds. Additionally, investigations into beam profile variations, corrections for motional mode couplings, as well as comparisons with other gate implementations are conducted, highlighting the efficiency and versatility of this frequency-stable gate method, and suggesting its potential for integrating multiple motional modes with various optical trap configurations, including balanced beam profiles within an ion trap array. Lastly, the connection to a broader framework of fault-tolerant quantum computing is also explored.

We discovered that the restricted distribution of $N$-gram models, resulting from their training approach, could be leveraged to enhance various language tasks. We developed a method called ResNGLM, which incorporates $N$-gram models within a neural framework to fine-tune existing pre-trained models for improved performance. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves notable results on a relatively new dataset called ATRC-3D, which is particularly challenging due to the extensive orientation variations and widespread occlusions present in its data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrfail/SADRNet.

This work delves into the underlying causes for the limitations of massive batch training. To overcome these constraints, the authors develop an alternative strategy. They demonstrate that, by alternating between smaller batches for efficient training and larger batches for data enrichment, they can achieve comparable performance to dedicated semi-supervised learning techniques while reducing labeling costs. The authors further expand upon this approach in a pivotal experiment, combining big batches with careful model fine-tuning, and successfully apply it to real-world images. The resulting method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques by a 1% margin on CIFAR-100 and matches the performance of semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. The code is available at github.com/DeepLearningAssistanceGroup/dynamic-learning.

Our investigation focused on the conductance properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized conductance pattern emerged when the chemical potential fell within the gapless region, due to the resonance of electrons within the Dirac cone. This led to conductance values equal to that of a full HgTe layer, as well as half-values, resulting from the presence of N-shaped or M-shaped conductance resonances, respectively. Examining large-sized samples revealed the presence of a sharp conductance minimum at the critical thickness, accompanied by zero-voltage conductance plateaus in samples with narrow widths. This threshold behavior could be altered by applying an electric field to change the gapless region's location, or by introducing impurities to break the spatial symmetry and induce resonant conductance. This led to various conductance scenarios, including multiple zero-voltage conductance plateaus in samples with medium widths. The importance of tunneling spectroscopy was also highlighted, as it allows for a more comprehensive examination of the electronic states within the conductance minimum. This research was conducted using low-temperature tunneling spectroscopy on HgTe quantum wells of varying thickness, and the resulting data was examined in relation to theoretical simulations. The outcomes have been quantified and presented in a set of figures accompanying this paper. The underlying physics has been discussed in a supplementary document available online. The examination of mesoscopic effects on the conductance of HgTe quantum wells is a promising area of investigation that can be integrated with existing studies of mesoscopic effects in other materials, and may also have implications for the utilization of HgTe quantum wells in quantum information technology. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule their own downlink and uplink time blocks based on local traffic patterns, leading to performance issues due to imbalanced load distribution. To address this, a new scheduling approach uses a dynamic TDD model where cells compete against each other in a non-cooperative game to optimize their own performance and overall system stability. Mathematical analysis shows that this approach results in a Nash Equilibrium, allowing efficient cellular loading to be derived. Furthermore, performance gains can be achieved through the optimization of a single scheduling parameter. A novel algorithm is also developed to track changes in the cellular loading and adjust TDD blocks accordingly. A comparative study with static TDD and alternative scheduling methods demonstrates the proposed approach's effectiveness. A pilot implementation on Dynamic TDD software defines the basics of its API and provides an example of a simple scheduler. A discussion on possible enhancements and a path forward for future work are also presented. A software implementation of the proposed algorithm for OpenAirInterface is introduced, along with a load balancing feature based on user location. A theoretical and empirical load distribution model is derived, showing that a dynamic TDD system can be highly efficient, with a nearly uniform load distribution achievable in a variety of scenarios. A proposal for a hybrid static and dynamic TDD approach is also presented, along with a loading threshold that balances the performance and overhead of dynamic TDD. A discussion on the possible applications and performance gains of this approach in 5G and LTE systems is also given. In this work, we introduce a novel method to train neural networks that can differentiate their inputs, which we call Hamiltonian Neural Differentiators. These unique networks, based on Hamiltonian control theory, generate outputs that determine the direction in which the input changes, effectively providing derivatives in the process. We discovered that these neural differentiators can be both the controllers and observers of time-varying systems and that they are sensitive to changes in the system dynamics. As a result, they can be trained to accurately predict derivatives for a wide range of systems, even in the presence of noise. We successfully applied our Hamiltonian Neural Differentiators to various systems, including complex nonlinear and time-varying systems, and found that they significantly outperformed traditional methods based on neural networks. We believe this breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize artificial intelligence, particularly in fields like robotics and finance, where derivatives play a crucial role. In the process, we also uncovered a key challenge that could impact the scalability of these systems. The code for the Hamiltonian Neural Differentiators is available at https://github.com/ghassang/hamiltonian-neural-differentiator.

As artificial intelligence technology advances and Machine Learning (ML) models are widely applied in various sectors, the significance of trustworthiness in these models also grows in importance. We propose a collaborative framework for agents, consisting of a Score Agent responsible for calculating trust scores based on models' predictions and a Refine Agent that utilizes these scores to select and correct errors in the data, improving the models' performance. We evaluate our approach in a real-world scenario, utilizing a dataset from the OpenStreetMap platform to train a separate agent to rectify geographical location annotations, and found that it effectively enhances the accuracy of ML models. Our proposed framework can be applied to various sectors, where the sources of data are accessible and relatively stable, leading to reliable and efficient results. Our research showcases a novel, scalable method to increase the trustworthiness of ML models, without necessitating extensive retraining. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghasemigabeh/HTM.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a zero-shot or few-shot learning approach.  However, these successes primarily focus on leveraging general language properties without accounting for the specific semantic details included in gloss context.  Our investigation reveals that gloss context is frequently overlooked, with many prior BERT-based methods yielding comparable performance to utilizing the full context.  We propose a novel framework, ContextGlossNet, incorporating a dual module that separately integrates context and gloss information before fusing them for WSD.  Experimental results on the Senseval and SemEval datasets demonstrate significant improvements, with average gains of 10.28% and 4.81% in exact match scores compared to the standard BERT baseline.  Our findings highlight the significance of distinguishing word senses based on gloss context and the effectiveness of a dual context-gloss integration approach in enhancing WSD accuracy.  We also analyze different context-gloss integration strategies and the influence of gloss quality on our method's performance.  Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang-nlp/ContextGlossNet.

This paper investigates the possibility of identifying top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at various energy levels through the analysis of certain variables, using proton-proton data as a reference point. A multiple variable approach is employed to differentiate between events containing top quarks and those that do not, with this method being applicable to a range of energies, including those beyond those accessible with the current LHC proton-proton data. The study takes into account the effects of hadronization, quark mass, and nuclear interactions on the analysis and provides estimates of the required collision energy to produce top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL understanding, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance filling, we propose a simple yet effective approach by integrating a task that predicts column names, demonstrating that column prediction facilitates filling by reducing ambiguity in target columns. To further improve performance, we employ a linear combination of column prediction losses to balance filling accuracy and efficiency. In addition, we find that training models on synthetic data with a modified auxiliary task enhances both schema linking and value filling performance. Our proposed approach and findings have been validated through a series of experiments using the Spider dataset, yielding superior performance in filling and comparable results in schema linking compared to the state-of-the-art approach, while demonstrating efficiency gains in complex datasets. Our code is available online at github.com/zwang-nlp/SpiderDECODE.

We define a new concept of a minimizing surface within a specific homotopy class in metric spaces with constant curvature. This kind of surface is not subject to boundary constraints and typically has unique properties that distinguish it from constant mean curvature surfaces. Our primary goal is to explore the structure of these surfaces and demonstrate the existence of minimizing surfaces within a homotopy class in metric spaces with positive curvature, thereby generalizing a previous result by G.M. Cicconellis. Additionally, we outline specific cases of minimizing surfaces in the context of hyperbolic geometry. The use we make of the term "minimizing" is in line with its conventional meaning within the field of geometric measure theory, and it is not related to the concept of mean curvature. The term "minimizing" in this context can be seen as a direct translation of the original Italian term "minimizzante". Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This pattern of shapes existing together together is particularly notable because it occurs at low spins, and is driven by a strong monopole interaction, counter to previous understanding that it only dominates at high spins, and primarily drives the formation of the 0+ ground state. This shape coexistence in 64Ni is also unique in that it differs from other known cases, such as 68Ni, where the interaction is balanced, making it an exciting and singular case that demands further investigation. This research was conducted by an international group of scientists, consisting of M. N. Tosh from the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in India, leading a group that included researchers from institutions such as Indiana University in the US, the University of Liverpool in the UK, the University of Ontario in Canada, the University of Cologne in Germany, the University of Warsaw in Poland, the University of York in the UK, the University of Edinburgh in the UK, the University of Jyvaskyla in Finland, the University of Helsinki in Finland, the University of Manchester in the UK, the University of Surrey in the UK, the University of Birmingham in the UK, the University of Tokyo in Japan, the University of Osaka in Japan, the University of Nishinihama in Japan, and the RIKEN Nishina Center in Japan.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces a large degree of uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, a small k is commonly employed to obtain an estimate of the model's ability to prevent overfitting, which can result in insufficient validation data and excessive variance in performance estimates. As a consequence, a smaller k may lead to suboptimal parameters and decreased model performance on unseen data. This paper investigates the impact of varying the fraction of data used for training and validation on model performance and demonstrates that using the k-fold cross-validation method mentioned above leads to excessive variance when tuning NLP models. As a solution, we propose switching to the method known as J-K fold CV, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments of the model via k-fold cross-validation and selecting the optimal parameters based on the results of N independent experiments. This approach is capable of reducing variance and leading to a better fit to the data, as seen in the experimental results presented. We prove that BI converges at rate O(1/t^2) under strong convexity and O(1/\sqrt(t))) under convexity, establishing the foundation for our main contribution – a two-stage procedure called BFWS. In stage one, BFWS produces a subgradient similar to iterative smoothing, while stage two refines this subgradient. We achieve better convergence rates of BI for convex objectives by leveraging the smoothness of the local predictor function, which we novelly define as Brief Function Representation. This representation bridges iterative smoothing and traditional convex optimization, enabling BI to surpass the performance of pure gradient descent for BI. Furthermore, we demonstrate that BI can solve large-scale constrained optimization problems by comparing our method with state-of-the-art interior-point methods. Lastly, we show that BFWS excels at MPE computation, outperforming other state-of-the-art algorithms, especially on large graphs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaleem/bi_biws.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme increase in resistance to flow that can often grind to a halt. Despite its surprising frequency, the underlying causes of shear thickening remain poorly understood, particularly in polymer-based materials. By examining a vast range of particle sizes, temperatures, and salt concentrations, we identified a precise, universal relationship governing the stresses at which shear thickening begins, a finding that holds true for a vast majority of particle-based fluids. Furthermore, we found that the width of this transition can be influenced by a range of factors, from random fluctuations to the extreme stress at which the fluid becomes nearly solid, and we developed a simple, universal metric to measure it. By analyzing the effects of changing conditions on stress transitions, we discovered that they often take on a distinctive, reversible pattern, and by combining our stress and image data, we found that the stresses at which these patterns shift can match those indicated by previous studies based solely on sound measurements. We define a new object called a "loom" to generalize the concept of a triangulation in combinatorial topology. Looms consist of a collection of edges in a circle, linked by rules that mimic the relationships found in triangulations. These links can twist and turn, yet remain stable, and their study leads to the discovery of a unique triangle in the center of the loom. This central triangle plays a significant role in converting a loom back into a triangulation. We establish a key relationship between looms and triangulations by demonstrating that any loom can be transformed into a triangulation through a process of subdivision. This process reveals that the geodesics within a loom are equivalent to the edges of its associated triangulation. Additionally, we find that the change in edge length among the loom's geodesics is directly related to the angle changes permitted in the underlying triangulation. This connection between looms and triangulations also leads to the discovery of a new concept called a "veering triangulation," characterized by straight geodesics rather than the typical curved edges found in standard triangulations. This advancement in understanding triangulations makes it possible to solve a previously unsolved problem in topology, known as Poincaré's Conjecture. We acknowledge that this achievement is a result of the contributions from many researchers, particularly Perelman's work using geometric reasoning. We propose that veering triangulations can be used to define a new concept of distance that varies with the choice of point, and that this distance can be utilized to prove Poincaré's Conjecture. We also explore the relationship between looms and triangulations at the level of their surfaces, which leads to the discovery of a new object called a "veering surface." We establish that the veering surface is independent of the choice of surface in three-dimensional space and that it retains the same topological characteristics. We propose that veering surfaces can be used to define a new concept of distance that varies with the choice of point, and that this distance can be utilized to prove Poincaré's Conjecture. We acknowledge that Perelman previously solved Poincaré's Conjecture using geometric reasoning in 2003, and our work on looms and veering surfaces is an alternative demonstration of this fact. Initially, we consider the Standard Model as the primary perturbation. We introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised scene flow estimation, leveraging metric learning and adversarial training to concentrate on ambiguous data points, thereby enhancing the estimation accuracy. We also explore the applicability of our benchmark to real-world downstream tasks, demonstrating the practical usefulness of 3D scene flow trajectories. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call policy learning in containerized microservices. During operation, Timeloops enables autonomous system call policy learning through a modular, lightweight timer-based system call monitoring approach. This technique compares the system calls made by containers within a short time frame to establish a baseline, thereby determining allowable system calls and preventing policy breaches. In addition to preventing breaches, Timeloops also identifies new system calls that could lower performance or security risks and submits them to the developer for review. We have implemented Timeloops on top of the Linux operating system and have tested its functionality using real-world applications including the Apache Kafka messaging system. Our results show that Timeloops yields a high level of accuracy, surpassing existing system call learning solutions by a 35% margin. Moreover, Timeloops' lightweight design enables it to operate efficiently without compromising performance, despite increasing memory usage slightly. Our data also indicate that Timeloops' capacity to detect performance-optimization opportunities opens up new avenues for research and could result in performance gains of as much as 30% in certain instances. We have made Timeloops available as an open-source tool on GitHub. Our findings have significant implications for the secure and efficient deployment of containerized microservices and we propose possible research directions in this area. Recent evidence suggests that the VTC's animacy structure comprises a continuous gradient, with the central region distinguishing living substances from non-living ones, and the polar regions differentiating between animals and plants. In this study, a multi-modal analysis of the VTC's animacy organization is explored through the integration of functional connectivity data, electrophysiological recordings, and computational modeling. Utilizing a novel approach that combines connection-weighted connectivity analysis with electrophysiological recording data, our results reveal that the VTC's animacy structure is characterized by a binary divide, with the central region enforcing a dichotomy based on animacy. A subsequent multi-agent neural network model is then applied to uncover the fundamental principles governing the VTC's animacy organization. Our findings indicate that a simple neural network composed of competitive hidden units is capable of capturing the VTC's animacy structure, with the central region's dichotomous classification enabled by a novel phenomenon known as the "exclusion effect." This study's results, ranging from the findings of the VTC's animacy continuum to the underlying mechanisms of the VTC's animacy structure, are validated through the analysis of a vast linguistic corpus, further demonstrating the empirical validity of the proposed neural network model. This revised logic, also known as QRE, enables the sound justification of quantifications relating to programs' behavior, achieving this through the validation of the program's ability to satisfy its specifications, as determined by the satisfaction of the truth of postconditions given the input and output. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. The appendices include realistic simulation scenarios that mimic various real-life scenarios, such as an early super-spreader event similar to that seen in Wuhan in 2020, a regular spread where the transmission rate is constant, and a comparison with the basic reproduction number $R_0$ in a naive model. The appendices also provide a mathematical derivation of effective $R_0$ values in different scenarios. The underlying assumptions of these models, along with their limitations, are discussed in depth. The appendices conclude with an analysis of a simple birth-death process that may be relevant to understanding the dynamics of epidemics in various settings. The appendices further explore this idea in the form of an extended case study. It is demonstrated that, despite the precision of vector magnetic field estimation, potential biases exist, particularly in the $B_\theta$ component, which could be attributed to the assumption that the magnetic field is nearly horizontal in the image integration process. The paper also explores potential sources of bias, including the application of the 180-degree ambiguity removal technique in vector data and the effect of the coordinate system used. A key challenge in training neural network models with periodic boundary conditions, as seen in many quantum many-body simulations, is the "sign issue" problem. This issue arises when the neural network learns a complex phase that varies across the spatial dimensions, leading to an exponential increase in the number of parameters and model complexity. To address this problem, we introduce a novel neural network architecture that utilizes complex weights and units only within local, fully connected layers, while keeping the remaining layers real-valued. By restricting the complex phase learning to a limited spatial range, we prevent the sign issue from emerging. Furthermore, this model allows for a significant reduction in model complexity compared to complex neural network alternatives. In our numerical experiments using a neural network with a U(1) symmetry, we found that the proposed model yields comparable accuracy to complex neural network models, while exhibiting a sign issue of less than 2.058. We also apply this model to simulate a Hubbard model at finite temperatures and half-filling, and obtain accurate results with a strong convergence in the imaginary time. This model can be utilized in a wide range of many-body simulations, particularly in simulations that involve finite temperatures and periodic boundary conditions. We have open-sourced the proposed model on GitHub, available for public use.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method yields consistent improvements in results across various evaluation metrics and datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.
For instance, in the Amazon Review Full dataset, ReCross achieves 0.85% to 1.05% increases in intrinsic scores and 0.5% to 1.5% gains in extrinsic scores compared to the baseline.
Our method's versatility is further illustrated by integrating ReCross with existing regularization techniques, leading to enhanced results in both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation tasks. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/ASD5/Automatic-Cross-Task-Improvement.

We used two approaches to create residual maps: one was based on a Gaussian mixture model and the other used a machine learning algorithm to detect anomalies. We applied these methods to data from the APOGEE-2 survey and focused on a representation of the chemical elements. The residual maps revealed patterns associated with various populations in the galaxy. We interpreted these patterns by comparing observed residuals with those predicted by stellar population models. We found that the models could accurately account for the behavior of chemically normal and abnormal stars in the galaxy's disk. However, there were aspects that the models couldn't explain, such as the abundance of aluminum-66 and the magnitude of scatter in the residuals. We also analyzed the properties of specific populations, such as young stellar groups near the sun and a group of stars with abnormal aluminum levels. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a simple yet effective strategy called the efficient loss selection method, leveraging a single network to efficiently discover a customized loss function across a broad spectrum of possible choices, resulting in performance gains of up to 6.8% in our experiments. Our work is accessible to the broader deep learning community due to the model's simple integration into existing frameworks. Our research highlights the significance of treating loss function as a parameter that can be optimized, rather than a fixed constant, as evidenced by the efficient loss selection method's promising performance gains. This research aims to simulate the mechanical impact and resulting temperature changes associated with strain-induced crystallization (SIC) during large-scale tire production, specifically focusing on a rubber compound that undergoes SIC. To accomplish this, a numerical methods framework was utilized to solve various problems, including heat transfer, mechanical deformation, and the kinetic rate of crystallization. A special feature of this model allows for the assessment of kinetic rate equations using experimental data from dynamic thermal analyzes of rubber samples with different crystallization rates. To apply this model to realistic tire manufacturing scenarios, a finite element representation was created, incorporating a temperature-dependent material model and a contact surface model for tire rollers. To validate the simulation results, a study was conducted on a rubber block experiencing repeated deformation, and the findings were compared to experimental data involving the microstructure and surface temperature changes. Furthermore, a numerical optimization was performed to increase the rate of SIC in the tire compound, by adjusting filler content. The results showed that adding a specific amount of filler can raise the kinetic rate of SIC, and this was confirmed through experimental analysis. The model was then utilized to investigate temperature and mechanical stress impacts on the kinetics of SIC, revealing its potential to optimize tire compound formulations that resist SIC-induced failures. The research was conducted in collaboration with Michelin, and the findings associated with the model's application to tire manufacturing were utilized to enhance the process. The developed method has the potential to be applied to other industrial processes involving the crystallization of isotropic materials. The model includes multiple kinetic rate equations for various compounds, and it can also be adapted to simulate surface-related reactions by modifying the kinetics rate equations. The research was funded by the Michelin group. The project involved collaboration with Michelin researchers, specifically Thomas Dumas, who is also listed as a co-author. The material costs and time associated with the simulation and experimental testing of tire compound SIC were substantial, as evidenced by the associated costs listed in the paper. The research involved a team of scientists and engineers from various backgrounds, including mechanical engineering, materials science, and chemistry. The project lasted for approximately 5 years, during which the researchers overcame significant challenges to achieve the results presented in the paper. The research was conducted to address industrial concerns related to tire compound formulations and the process of strain-induced crystallization. The simulation model developed in the paper can be applied to other industrial processes involving the crystallization of isotropic materials, and it has the potential to be adapted for surface-related reactions by modifying the kinetics rate equations.

We investigate the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, specifically focusing on the interplay between magnetization and nematic effects on the $k$-dependent $d$-vector spin structure. Our comprehensive study, utilizing a combination of experimental observations and theoretical analysis, emphasizes the significance of considering magnetization-induced anisotropic modifications to the $d$-vector. These modifications lead to (i) anisotropic expansion of the nematic phase, (ii) rotation of the $d$-vector components, and (iii) distinct behaviors of Pauli paramagnetic responses at high-symmetry points. Experimental evidence is obtained from magnetization and specific heat measurements, supporting theoretical predictions and revealing distinctive signatures of spin-triplet nematic superconductivity. Furthermore, our findings imply that the (possibly realized) spin-triplet nematic state in Ti-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ would exhibit unique responses to external pressure and strain, influenced by the anisotropic lattice strain effects on the $d$-vector components. This study provides a framework for interpreting and predicting magnetic and thermal responses in various materials with spin-triplet nematic or other $d$-vector configurations. This work is also relevant to related materials, such as strontium-doped BaNi$_2$P$_3$ and Eu-doped Gd$_2$CuO$_4$, which may exhibit (or have been incorrectly identified as exhibiting) spin-triplet nematic behavior. This study highlights the importance of considering magnetization-induced anisotropic effects on the $d$-vector components, and it demonstrates that the specific anatomy of the $d$-vector vector can be determined through theoretical and experimental analysis of the anisotropic responses to external pressure and strain. This can be achieved by matching the anisotropic responses to the predicted behaviors of the Pauli paramagnetic responses, specifically the anisotropic dependencies of the specific heat, magnetic anisotropy, and elastic strain effects on the $d$-vector components. This approach enables the distinction between spin-triplet nematic and isotropic configurations, as well as the determination of the $d$-vector anatomy in various materials. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common-sense reasons both for and against performing various actions, described in straightforward "if-then" statements. This dataset distinguishes itself from existing sources of common sense by focusing on conditional relationships rather than individual facts and scenarios. With over 140,000 descriptive statements covering around 300 diverse actions, ATOMIC offers significant challenges for the next generation of artificial intelligence models, particularly in if-then reasoning, and provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating them. We present five novel datasets derived from this core framework, each tailored to a specific aspect of if-then reasoning, and demonstrate improved performance of various machine intelligence models on these datasets. We also reveal the limitations of current models in if-then reasoning and highlight areas for future development. With its unique structure and extensive coverage, ATOMIC offers valuable insights into the workings of machine intelligence and provides a valuable tool for further advancing this technology. We publicly release ATOMIC at https://atOMIC.github.io.

One of the most significant advantages of quantum computing lies in its capacity to accelerate linear algebraic problems through iterative linear solvers, particularly the use of the Quantum Linear Algebra (QuLA) framework. However, due to limited quantum resources, certain operations can't be performed in the conventional way used in classical computers, such as the use of Hadamard transforms in the QuLA framework. To address this challenge, we propose modifying the QuLA framework to incorporate alternative matrix multiplication methods, specifically using the t-Duffeling matrix transformation, which can be more efficient for noisy, intermediate-scale quantum systems. We also explore the potential benefits of combining the QuLA framework with classical linear solvers, including the t-Duffeling transformation, to achieve greater quantum performance. To support our claims, we provide a detailed analysis of the modified QuLA framework as well as examples of linear system solving using the tDuffeling transformation and the QuLA framework in combination with the classical Conjugate Gradient method. Our findings indicate that there is a sweet spot for the number of quantum bits required to achieve optimal performance, and that using the Conjugate Gradient method in conjunction with the QuLA framework in combination with the tDuffeling transformation on a 32-qubit system yields an approximate 20% reduction in execution time compared to the conventional approach. Our research is significant because it provides a method for extending the QuLA framework to work with noisy, intermediate-scale quantum systems, and demonstrates the potential for combining the QuLA framework with classical linear solvers to achieve greater quantum performance. Our findings also highlight the potential for performance improvements in systems with limited quantum resources, and our research can be applied to a wide range of linear algebraic problems, including the solution of linear systems, matrix approximation, and kernel methods.
