Given any real number p greater than 1 and any integer q greater than 1, this paper defines a new notion called p/q-identifiable sets within the context of number theory, specifically within the realm of integer arrays and quadratic forms. It then demonstrates the connection between these sets and a prominent Diophantine equation, as well as establishes criteria for any subset of the natural numbers to be considered p/q-identifiable. Furthermore, it proves a p/q-identifiable set will necessarily have a specific distributional characteristic, mirroring a consequence initially discovered by the Polish mathematician Sierpiński for a different class of numbers. Additionally, it demonstrates that certain well-known classes of numbers are p/q-identifiable, yet not (1+sqrt(5))/2-identifiable. Lastly, it shows any subset of the natural numbers that is distributed in a particular random manner is not p/q-identifiable, thereby establishing a distinction between deterministic and random number arrays. This work was presented initially at the 2010 Combinatorics and Number Theory Conference held in Budapest.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for strong consistency, high availability, and high performance in various applications. Despite its popularity, verifying the consistency characteristics of MongoDB has been subject to debate among database and concurrency experts. Proving the consistency properties of MongoDB involves complex concurrency control and cache coherence analysis. This paper demonstrates the application of formal methods to validate the consistency characteristics of MongoDB, specifically its transactional coherence, using the specification language TLA+. A previous study attempted to formalize MongoDB's consistency properties but was found to contain errors. This paper corrects those flaws and provides a more accessible verification approach. By using a style similar to MongoDB's source code, this paper shows that MongoDB's transactional coherence can be validated through a simple and intuitive implementation of cache coherence protocols. This approach allows for easy extension to investigate MongoDB's latest versions, such as MongoDB 5.0. This verification process can be difficult as it involves complex concurrency control and cache coherence analysis but can be facilitated by dividing the investigation into multiple components, including but not limited to: concurrency control within transactions, snapshotting, locking, and cache coherence protocols. This paper presents a reusable framework that enables easy examination of MongoDB's consistency characteristics for its various components and versions. This verification process demonstrates that MongoDB ensures that cached documents that have been updated in one session are not returned as up-to-date in another session that has accessed the same dataset. This ensures that updates made to cached documents in one session are propagated to the cache of another session that has accessed the same dataset. This paper also presents a corrected version of the TLA+ specifications that were previously published, along with an executable model that allows for easy exploration of MongoDB's consistency characteristics for its various components and versions. This model demonstrates that MongoDB ensures that cached documents that have been updated in one session are not returned as up-to-date in another session that has accessed the same dataset. This ensures that updates made to cached documents in one session are propagated to the cache of another session that has accessed the same dataset. Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka array from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that the expanded class includes functions associated with Kostka numbers, thereby extending the result from Cho-Huh (2019) to a broader context. We also uncover a subarray of the inverse Kostka array that possesses a particular symmetry, which we further verify occurs within the context of the expanded class. Additionally, our analysis reveals the $e$-positivity of the expanded class when using the monotone symmetric function basis, providing a distinct expansion that differs from the one based on the elementary symmetric function basis. We explore and validate the correctness of our combinatorial interpretations through numerical computations and comparisons with established results. Furthermore, our analysis establishes a link between the expanded class and the M\"obius function of the weak order on the Young diagram corresponding to the related partition, which we prove via the application of the branch operator and the analysis of the underlying combinatorial structures. We also explore and validate the correctness of our findings through numerical computations and comparisons with established results. Finally, our analysis enables us to derive explicit and expansive expansions for the modified Stanley symmetric functions of the referenced Dyck paths, which we achieve through the application of the branch operator and the analysis of the underlying combinatorial structures. We explore and validate the correctness of these expansions through numerical computations and comparisons with established results. We provide and validate a particular instance of such an expansion for the modified Stanley symmetric function corresponding to the sequence $\{3,3,2\}$, which includes the fundamental change of variables formula as a special case, as well as expansions for the modified Stanley symmetric functions corresponding to the sequences $\{3,2,2,1\}$ and $\{4,3,2\}$. We also explore and validate the correctness of these expansions through numerical computations and comparisons with established results. Research on dynamic complex systems often relies on either basic node connections or sophisticated geometric frameworks, but not often both, given the challenging integration of these approaches. Here, we take a novel concealed geometry strategy, where a complex system's geometric structure is inferred from the assembly's topological properties. Incorporating this method into a recent model that accounts for both pairwise and triangular interactions, we successfully recover the original geometric parameters and characteristics of the network. Utilizing triangle-based interactions proves particularly crucial in defining the network's topology and assembling the geometry correctly. We demonstrate this approach on a model showing first-order phase transitions and geometric changes, including spin reversal through N-K oscillations. The proposed concealed geometry method provides a valuable tool for uncovering a network's underlying geometry in complex systems, offering a promising means of exploring hidden dimensions in complex networks. We investigated the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere using data from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on board Parker Solar Probe during its first 7 orbits. The research focused on analyzing scalar solar wind speed, density, and magnetic and electric field strengths to calculate the energy flux throughout the inner heliosphere. The data revealed a positive correlation between energy flux and solar wind speed, as well as an inverse relationship between energy flux and proximity to the sun. Furthermore, the data showed that the energy flux remains consistent with values obtained from orbts 2-7 near the 1.15 solar radius landmark, where the solar wind is likely affected by the solar breeze feedback mechanism. The observations from Parker Solar Probe provided the first data on the solar wind energy flux so close to the sun and offered a initial look at the energy flux distribution within the inner heliosphere. The findings also offer a basis for examining the solar wind energy flux distribution in the inner heliosphere and offer a chance to investigate the influence of the solar breeze on the solar wind density within this region. The research was conducted in collaboration with the Parker Solar Probe Comprehensive Wave Investigation team. The data analysis utilized custom-written code in the IDL language in addition to publicly available code. This approach, known as time-series clustering, groups sequences of data into clusters based on their underlying dynamics, ignoring the time dimension. In this study, we applied time-series clustering to analyze the sound generated during the peeling of an adhesive tape. Surprising patterns emerged when researchers compared the clustered signals to mathematical models of noise, revealing a hidden structure in the data that refutes a long-standing assumption about random sound caused by friction. This assumption holds that such noise always lacks a pattern and is therefore indistinguishable from noise in statistical terms. Consequently, we found that the sound during tape peeling can be distinguished from random noise even when time series data is analyzed. To validate this finding, we used a separate method to estimate the accuracy of this result, and also demonstrated that the sound during tape peeling originates from a specific mechanical source, thereby confirming the connection between this noise and crackling sounds that occur due to mechanical failure within materials. This research provides an important example of how noise that appears random can actually have a underlying meaning, offering insights that can be applied to other physical systems where noise is present. When applying the Weyl semimetal theory to real-world materials, it's common to encounter issues due to over-reliance on linearized dispersion relationships. A non-linear Weyl semimetal theory has been developed to address these challenges by incorporating non-linear momentum dependencies into the Chern number calculation. This approach eliminates overestimating the Weyl semimetal's stability and allows for the description of multiple Weyl points, all of which can be simultaneously critical. A new, non-linear theory of non-abelian Weyl semimetals has now been introduced, which can be applied to real-world materials by calculating robust Dirac fermion states via k-space averaging and Chern number calculations using a suitable volume of k-space. This non-linear framework also makes it possible to determine the temperature dependence of the Weyl semimetal's stability in a range of models, including a 3D generalization of a type of Weyl semimetal known as a double-well semimetal. This non-linear approach shows that the distance between a double-well semimetal's Weyl points decreases in proportion to the reduction of the bulk Dirac cone's size due to finite temperature effects. In particle accelerators, knowing the position and shape of the beam is crucial for ensuring efficiency and minimizing the risk of equipment damage. Since beam detectors are often limited to measuring within a specific area, researchers are exploring innovative methods to determine the beam's intensity across its entire path. This paper introduces a novel approach, called brightness scanning, that uses a slowly moving beam in conjunction with a fixed detector to determine the distribution of intensity across the particle beam. We demonstrate that collecting and analyzing data from a particle detector as the beam moves can provide a precise, two-dimensional image of the intensity distribution. However, we also show that this data contains redundant information that needs to be accounted for to accurately reconstruct the beam's distribution. We then outline a strategy to preprocess the data effectively, eliminating the redundancy and facilitating an accurate reconstruction of the intensity distribution. This method can be applied to various beam configurations and has been particularly successful in diagnosing high-intensity particle beams used in linear accelerators and storage rings. In such contexts, evaluating the shape of the beam is crucial, and we propose a statistical method that can be used to assess the distribution accurately. In addition to its applications in linear accelerators and storage rings, brightness scanning can also be used to detect asymmetries in beam formation, determine the distribution of intensity along the direction of particle motion, and evaluate the shape of the beam in linear accelerators used in storage ring configurations. We have successfully tested this approach using both numerical simulations and experimental data collected from the Advanced Photon Source. In these experiments, we moved the beam manually to demonstrate the feasibility of brightness scanning in real-world settings and found that collecting 1000 sets of data was sufficient to accumulate a high-fidelity image of the intensity distribution. We also examined the effectiveness of this method for beam diagnostics in linear accelerators and found that collecting data from a detector as the beam moves can provide the information needed to determine the distribution of intensity across the particle beam, even with a detector that is fixed in place. We have made several enhancements to this approach, including developing a mathematical model of the beam that can be used to predict the intensity distribution, using this model to guide the collection of data, and using statistical methods to evaluate the shape of the beam. We have applied this method to a linear accelerator and a storage ring and have successfully used it to detect asymmetries in beam formation, determine the distribution of intensity along the direction of particle motion, and evaluate the shape of the beam in linear accelerators used in storage ring configurations. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. The findings can be applied to a wide range of real-world problems, including smart grids and supply chains, where the presence of malicious actors could have severe consequences. The research also uncovers interesting insights into the trade-off between compression and trustworthiness in the context of robust optimization. The proposed algorithm has been shown to be adaptable to dynamic environments, where the set of trustworthy agents can change over time. The study also delves into the energy efficiency of the proposed algorithm, emphasizing the critical role of node degree in the graph constructed through communication between agents. The research has been published in the journal IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics, Volume 16, Issue 1, January 2020. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with multiple detectors. As such, achieving an accurate and precise measurement demands a thorough understanding and proper accounting of instrumental effects on the data, particularly frequency-dependent biases that can manifest as systematic errors. A new Python package, s4cmb, is presented with the aim of simulating instrumental biases in cosmic microwave background experiments. It facilitates the generation of randomized signals reflecting the anomalous signals believed to exist based on prior research, as well as the random allocation of biased signals to sky maps with associated uncertainty estimates. The package's capabilities are demonstrated by analyzing a mock data set representing the BICEP/Keck Array Experiment, and the implications of instrumental biases on parameter estimation were calculated, revealing that, in the context of this experiment, the bias likely amounts to a few percent on large-scale anisotropies and primary foregrounds, and could potentially reach ten percent on smaller scales and point sources. The results further indicate that the bias's impact on parameter estimation could be significant, with variations ranging from a few percent to over a hundred percent, and that a more precise estimation of the bias's magnitude is crucial for accurately interpreting future data sets. The s4cmb package is an open-source tool available for public use, and developers are encouraging contributions from the community to enhance the package's features. The package can be utilized in its current form to analyze existing data sets and future experiments, with a future planned expansion to include the simulation of instrumental biases in foreground removal methods. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable deepfake detection method. Deepfake techniques, originating from the generation of cosmetic alterations, have progressed to employ advanced networking techniques such as cross-stitching in multiple domains. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel detection framework titled MD-CSDNetwork, which incorporates a two-part mechanism to identify deepfakes. Firstly, a network is trained to distinguish between real and synthetic images, and this training is used to create a dataset for the second part, which involves training a classifier to separate deepfake and genuine images using an ABN-based mechanism. We also examine the efficacy of our framework for both single-domain and multiple-domain experiments, and our findings are comparable to the current state-of-the-art. MD-CSDNetwork, our proposed method, employs a straightforward and scalable technique to detect high-quality deepfakes, especially those created using cross-stitching techniques in multiple domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/abhishekKumbhar/MD-CSDNetwork.

We introduce a new framework where cluster algebras are integrated into geometric terms, specifically within the context of projective lines and their extensions to flag varieties. We demonstrate how this integration leads to a characterization of the cluster structure associated with the Lusztig quantum group $\mathbb{C}_q(G)$ through the use of $\mathbb{Z}$-orbit forms. Fraudulent schemes on blockchain networks have grown in complexity, enabling con artists to exploit naive users with ease. This research examines the structure and operation of Forsage, a highly successful and widely promoted pseudo-peaceful scam conducted on the Ethereum network. By analyzing game participants' roles, understanding how users were deceived, and tracing the flow of stolen funds, this study reveals the financial gains enjoyed by perpetrators and identifies key transaction patterns associated with fraudulent activities. Furthermore, we identify a discrepancy in transaction classification used by previous studies and propose a more accurate method of calculating scam-related transactions. With the rise of simple and complex scams on the horizon, this study also explores theoretical variations of these scams, including a new scheme called the "Stealing Game." Lastly, we provide actionable advice to blockchains, online platforms, and advertising companies to prevent fraudulent schemes from succeeding. This research is applicable to various blockchain networks, including Ethereum. In particular, Ethereum allows anyone to create and distribute a smart contract automatically, which has contributed to the proliferation of scams on this platform. With total scam-related transactions valued at over $2 billion on Ethereum alone, this issue demands urgent attention. This study offers valuable insights to researchers, while also providing a useful tool to platforms, companies, and individuals interested in identifying and preventing scams. In addition, it provides a theoretical framework for game theory related to peaceful scams, which can be used as a reference by scholars. This research was conducted by reviewing Forsage-related online content, analyzing Ethereum blockchain data, as well as conducting surveys and interviews with Forsage participants. This study is novel in that it is the first to thoroughly examine the structure and operation of Forsage, which has enabled it to contribute new knowledge to the field. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have published the research in the form of a catalog featuring the basic properties of the newly discovered candidate clusters along with a detailed examination of their possible membership among the galaxy's bulge globular cluster population.

In 2019, a novel holographic tensor network model was proposed, featuring tensor bonds that display rotational invariance and approximate holographic entropy equality. This class of networks were termed "hyper-invariant MERA" due to their invariant properties under the rotation of their tensor bonds. A significant discovery has been made about the capacity of these networks to accurately encode and recover information. Specifically, it has been found that their recovery channels effectively resemble quantum holographic error-correcting codes when based on power-law dependencies. The effectiveness of these networks in recovering information can be assessed through the quantum entanglement renormalization group theory, while their error-correcting capabilities can be evaluated using the holographic Hamiltonian truncation method. Both of these analysis methods support the notion that hyper-invariant MERA models represent powerful tools for approximating holographic error-correcting codes, particularly in their ability to handle a vast range of power-law dependencies. Nonetheless, there are instances where these models fall short, and alternative approaches may be necessary for their improvement. The application of these models to realistic scenarios is also discussed, including their use in coupling a quantum system to a noisy environment and their ability to break down in critical situations, often resulting in the loss of their holographic properties. The hyper-invariant MERA models have been compared to other tensor network architectures, revealing that their holographic properties can be distinguished, and demonstrating that their recovery channels display unique features, such as the destruction of holographic properties in certain regimes, and the formation of gap-like structures in their entropy spectra. The development of the quantum thermodynamics of these models has also been explored, yielding a new understanding of the relationship between their holographic properties and their thermal behavior. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of hyper-invariant MERA models, offering a promising tensor network architecture for the study of holographic theories, and providing a precise definition of these models that can be used as a starting point for future investigations. The paper contains three figures and one table, and the results have been tested using numerical simulations. The authors hope that this work will pave the way for future studies on the thermal behavior of these models and will contribute to a deeper understanding of holographic theories, as well as providing a feasible tensor network architecture for the investigation of holographic error-correcting codes, and presenting a novel approach to resolving the breakdown of these models in critical situations. The paper is addressed to the scientific community engaged in quantum many-body theory, with possible applications to related fields such as condensed matter physics and cosmology

A comprehensive model of near-ultraviolet spectral continuum has been developed for the 1985 superflare of AD Leo, incorporating measurements of photometric data and spectral analysis. This approach takes into account the effects of photospheric absorption, atmospheric scattering of ultraviolet light, and the structure of the stellar atmosphere, particularly the impact of the high-level activity in this G-type main-sequence star. To accurately represent the observed spectrum, a grid of detailed spectral models was used to construct a continuous continuum model for the UV band. This model has been applied to multiple observations of AD Leo, providing effective temperature and surface gravity estimates that remain unchanged, while revealing a stronger absorption by iron peptides due to increased surface activity. Conditional smoothing models like Conditional Spherical Gaussian (CSG) have shown significant improvements in treating noise in 3D point clouds. These models can input a noisy point cloud and output a smoothed cloud based on the underlying geometry, without being bound by grid-based restrictions. However, implementing learning-based CSG on a wide range of datasets is challenging due to high computational costs and memory requirements. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel UQ (Unique Q-function) Smoothing Framework that leverages a simple, grid-based learning platform to train a seamless and high-performance smoothing model, specifically for 3D point clouds. This Framework utilizes a unique Q-function that is invariant to specific transformation applications, resulting in a smooth and memory-efficient model that can be executed across various datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our UQ Smoothing Framework by applying it to multiple datasets across various resolution and noise levels. Specifically, we see a 5 times reduction in memory usage while maintaining a 90% similarity in reconstruction results when comparing our model to a baseline CSG model. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengChengSong/TPC.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect the complex structure of electric dipole resonances through the $^{16}$O nucleus case. Contrary to conventional assumptions, our results reveal that the resonances' widths derive not solely from the widths of individual RPA poles but rather stem from the complex dynamics of the RPA coefficients. Additionally, we find evidence for a phenomenon known as "avoided energy crossing," where two RPA poles interact with each other, causing a "frozen" width development that maintains a consistent distance between two distinct RPA states along a range of approximately 20 MeV. This interaction results in a distinctive hump structure that extends up to 25 MeV above the primary GDR peak and is observable in both electric monopole and dipole spectra of $^{16}$O. Our study highlights the intricate details of RPA poles and their impact on the broad, dense profiles of giant dipole resonances. Moreover, these findings are relevant to theoretical models that aim to understand the complex structures and widths of GDR states and can be applied to other nuclei by modifying the RPA framework and the $^{16}$O specific Jost function parameters. Our data for $^{16}$O is presented in Figs 1-4. Our results highlight the intricate dynamics of energy avoidance and the complex structure of GDR widths, and we propose several possible explanations for these phenomena, including the role of the $^{12}$C core's configuration, the RPA renormalization of the ground state, and the collective effects of the 4$\pi$ RPA field, which influences the dynamics of energy avoidance and the broadening of the GDR widths. These explanations are supported by the accompanying Figs 5-7. Our approach provides a precise analysis of the complex structure of GDR widths and the dynamics of energy avoidance, and we believe it can be applied to other nuclei by modifying the RPA framework and the Jost function parameters. In this research, we develop an innovative clustering method called Impact Based Clustering (IBC) to analyze complex systems whose behavior changes over time. We distinguish static elements like structures and relationships, and dynamic aspects like variables that evolve across time and space. The IBC approach groups systems based on the changes that occur within their components over time, rather than the structures themselves. A significant aspect of IBC is a new metric called the Spatial-Temporal Impact (STI) measure, which determines the level of change within a system by calculating the difference between its current and previous states across different locations. The IBC method uses the STI measure to identify these levels of change and develops a decision-making framework to identify clusters and preferred policies by applying game theory and learning from data. We test the efficacy of IBC on a simulated example and a real-world energy consumption dataset, and find that it outperforms existing clustering methods in terms of policy evaluation scores. The results also demonstrate that IBC's ability to handle temporal dependencies and data-driven learning from experience allows it to yield more accurate predictions and better policy recommendations compared to alternative methods. The code for IBC is available online.

In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained significant ground in natural language processing tasks like text generation. However, achieving optimal performance from these models is challenging due to the difficulty in balancing training stability and generation quality. We introduce SparseGAN, a novel GAN architecture that combines sparsity constraints in both training and sampling processes to produce high-quality texts. During training, we introduce an additional constraint that prevents the discriminator from being too sophisticated, reducing the likelihood of oscillations that can lead to suboptimal solutions. We also implemented a cumulative distribution function-based discriminator that improves performance by reducing the number of meaningless samples generated by the discriminator. SparseGAN demonstrates superior performance over existing methods across a range of text generation tasks, as evident from the results obtained using standard evaluation metrics like BLEU-2, ROUGE, and CIDEr. We have open-sourced SparseGAN at the URL https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a method was developed to predict the fate of microbial life forms that could have been carried on a space rock, taking into account various astrophysical environments, including stars and planets, and the physical properties of both microorganisms and meteorites. By utilizing a statistical approach and combining data from multiple sources, including telescopes that study the spectrum of reflected light from nearby stars, meteorite arrival patterns on planetary surfaces can be inferred from exoplanetary systems. In a study of 1,000 calculated trajectories, patterns of meteorite arrivals were found to be influenced by the presence of high-mass stars, low-mass stars, and planetary orbits, among other factors. In particular, a notable increase in meteorite arrivals was observed on planets with orbital zones similar to that of Earth, in regions surrounding a 2.5-solar-mass star that has a strong gravitational pull and high surface temperature. If interstellar panspermia exists, then life forms should be able to survive on planets with orbital zones between 0.5 and 1.5 times the distance between the stars' inner edge and their tidal edges, which delimit the stable planetary orbits. In a survey of 2,600 exoplanetary systems, 12 systems with potentially life-bearing planets that have had contact with meteorites were identified, providing a starting point for further investigation and offering a feasible approach for detecting interstellar panspermia through astronomical means. In the future, this method can be applied to a larger dataset of exoplanetary systems, with an estimated 10,000 systems awaiting discovery, which could lead to a much higher predicted rate of 10,000 potentially life-bearing planets with meteorite arrivals annually. The discovery of a microbial survivor on a planet that has had contact with meteorites could be confirmed through a combination of astronomical observations, by verifying the star's properties and the planet's orbital zone, and biological analysis, by investigating the meteorite's composition and the microorganism's genetic structure. The validation of interstellar panspermia would not only explain the presence of life on planets with stable orbits around certain stars but also provide evidence for a widespread, universal mechanism of life transfer, offering insights into the role of meteorites in shaping the evolution of life in various planetary systems. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a higher level of accuracy than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the transmission of solutions within multilayer networks composed of identically structured layers. By applying this approach to multilayer networks, we can establish conditions under which signals can be transmitted between layers, specifically in regards to the Kuramoto model. By analyzing a model with two layers, we demonstrate the transmission of dynamics from one layer to the other. Furthermore, we show that layers with different rotation speeds can also exchange signals, thereby affecting the nodes' rotation speeds. Ultimately, our findings on a double-layer network can be generalized to complex multilayer networks with many layers, each composed of numerous connected elements. The method we've introduced provides a means of investigating the transmission of signals within these complex networks, although the specific conditions of signal transmission remain an open question requiring further investigation. The code associated with this study is available online. In this study, the stress-strain relationship for an isotropic material is analyzed to demonstrate how the comprehensive Cauchy stress operator can be simplified to a second-order tensor, while maintaining consistency with experimental data. A statistical approach is employed to determine the basic parameters required to define the stress-strain relationship, and it is shown that the stress operator can be represented in terms of these simplified parameters in a gradient expansion. The proposed formulation is then applied to the analysis of a specific problem involving a material sample subjected to impact loading. The results obtained from the numerical simulations are compared with experimental observations of a specific material, known as 1020 steel, which has a complex stress-strain relationship but can be accurately represented by the proposed parameterization method. The statistical analysis of the simulation data reveals that the stress-strain relationship for this material can be characterized by a single parameter when considering plastic deformation, and it is demonstrated that the proposed method can effectively capture the nonlinear stress-strain behavior of this material. The proposed approach is also compared with the standard elastoplastic model, which is commonly used to model material behavior, and it is shown that the proposed method can capture nonlinear material behavior more accurately. The results of this study provide new insights into the analysis of material behavior and offer a valuable approach for modeling the nonlinear stress-strain relationships of materials. The method has been applied to the analysis of a specific material, but it has the potential to be extended to the investigation of other materials, including composite materials and biological tissues, which often exhibit complex nonlinear stress-strain relationships. The proposed method can be used in a variety of applications, including impact loading analysis, fracture prediction, and image-guided treatment, which involve the analysis of material behavior in a gradient field. The method provides a nonlinear operator approach to material modeling and offers a new perspective on the analysis of material behavior, which can be described using point operators and state variables. The proposed approach has been implemented using the Finite Element Method and the results of the numerical simulations are in close agreement with the experimental observations of the material sample. The method provides accurate results at a lower computational cost compared to the standard elastoplastic model and offers a level of precision that is comparable to the standard model but with a level of complexity that is lower. The proposed method offers a linearly stable formulation of the elastoplastic problem and it is free from instability issues that are associated with the standard elastoplastic model. Our paper presents a method for generating test data based on a geometric concept called "half-spaces". We demonstrate how to incorporate this method into existing testing processes, including classic methods and those using automated tools. Additionally, we show how to utilize this approach to identify areas for improvement in tested program components. This method can be applied to a broad range of programs, including complex, large-scale applications. Our analysis reveals that over-dependent reliance on formal verification techniques, such as proof-based approaches, is a limitation of this method. Nevertheless, we believe its practical value in developing and testing software makes it a valuable tool. Our method has been successfully tested with real-world programs, namely the operating system Unix and the programming language C, and is suitable for researchers and practitioners to use, offering a clear and straightforward procedure. Our method is also compatible with existing testing and validation frameworks, providing a practical solution for developing dependable software. Our approach to testing aims to minimize the number of test cases needed, while ensuring that generated cases are effective in revealing errors. without using detection equipment or traffic flow models. A combinatorial
approach is taken to analyze data from probe vehicles, which are inferred to
have been in queues based on their speed recordings. A priority rule causes
these probes to sort among each other by their estimated delay lengths, allowing
the application of the bubble sort algorithm to determine the distribution
of delay lengths. The study includes empirical testing of the method using data
from the I-81 Intelligent Highway System, which shows that it effectively estimates

delay distributions. Furthermore, the results indicate that the method's performance

vehicles. The method has a minimal requirement for initial parameters and is

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our new approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand this novel method, offering users an intuitive interface for exploring advanced numerical techniques and providing tools for visualizing solution progress and metric quantities. Despite the proposed approach's effectiveness, the signature of the spacetime metric remains uncertain, overdetermined systems may occur, and solutions might not be unique, implying the need for additional constraints or new methods to address these issues. Nonetheless, the CTTK scheme offers a valuable alternative for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in numerical relativity. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/JasonBodewits/CTTK.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We observe an unusual temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN thin films, potentially linked to the interplay between electronic free carriers and remote dopants. Given the material's sensitivity to post-deposition treatment and oxidation, we find that annealing in nitrogen gas leads to a decrease in conductivity and a significant increase in the anomalous Nernst coefficient, resulting in a notable shift in the temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst effect from a minimum to a maximum. Our results demonstrate the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN thin films and highlight the potential for manipulating the anomalous Nernst coefficient through interplanar coupling and remote dopants, offering a promising avenue for further exploration. Moreover, this study emphasizes the importance of considering the complex interplay between electronic free carriers and remote dopants in magnetic materials and the necessity of precise experimental Hall coefficient measurements. Given the experimental challenges involved, we propose a method for calculating the anomalous Nernst coefficient from the Hall effect and magnetotransport measurements, allowing for a comparison with theoretical models and simulations. The pandemic accelerated the shift to remote scientific collaborations, highlighting the need for more flexible access to user facilities. To address this, the integration of machine learning, automation, and advanced instrumentation is transforming user facilities, enabling high-throughput and distant operation. This movement is intertwined with a new paradigm of data-driven science, where computational resources are centered around massive datasets and repositories of observational data. In this paper, we outline a framework for designing and optimizing experiments in user facilities, specifically focusing on the example of magnetometer sensors in the Magnetic Resonance Imaging facility. We demonstrate how machine learning can optimize experimental settings, reduce measurement time, and accurately predict outcomes, thus increasing the efficiency of user facilities. By integrating this approach, we can combine the strengths of automated experimentation and machine learning to facilitate flexible, remote operation and exploit the potential of user facilities to their fullest capacity. This effort is a part of a broader initiative to develop a more open and collaborative data access policy, combined with the development of high-performance interfaces for secure remote operation. This work is particularly relevant to facilities like Magnetic Resonance Imaging, Magnetic Ionization, and X-ray facilities, with similar applications possible in other user facilities across various fields. This work is a submission for the Machine Learning for Physical Sciences Workshop at NeurIPS 2023.

To effectively address questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate rich external knowledge. However, utilizing vast amounts of knowledge often results in unnecessary information that hinders question answering performance. To streamline the process, we introduce a method called Coarse-to-Careful (C2C) that initializes question answers through a less stringent semantic search, followed by a more rigorous assessment incorporating multiple details from knowledge sources. The C2C framework leverages a novel strategy to fuse semantic-related information from knowledge graphs and incorporates a distinct approach to evaluate the credibility of knowledge excerpts. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various knowledge sources, including large-scale knowledge graphs and abstracts from academic papers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the C2C approach by incorporating it into a question answering framework, and our results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the CommonsenseQA dataset. Moreover, we showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to the Scientific Commonsense Question Answering dataset, and our results indicate that it also excels on this dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

Astronomical environments are vulnerable to destruction by extreme UV and high-energy particle bombardment, which readily break down molecules into cations. Although this process might seem destructive for forming new molecules, it actually facilitates the formation of molecular cations that can be formed into complementary anions. As a result, molecular cations with anions such as water, carbon dioxide, and ketones are likely common in space, yet their anionic counterparts remain unknown. This study seeks to investigate the absence of anionic cations in the solar system, focusing on an analysis of available cometary spectrum data. By examining the anionic cations that can be formed from pre-existing space components like hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur, we can infer the likely anionic cations that should exist but have not been discovered. Among these anionic cations, the oxygen-containing cations with the lowest ionization energies turn out to be the most elusive, presenting the greatest knowledge gaps in cometary spectra. Consequently, developing an understanding of these anionic cations is crucial for a more comprehensive comprehension of cometary matter, solar system chemistry, and the anionic cations that can be formed into complementary molecules. This knowledge is essential for advancing our understanding of the molecular anions that can be formed from interstellar space, as well as the anisotropic solar system environments that may be revealed through the study of molecular anions. This study highlights the significance of conducting further observations with a focus on detecting the anionic cations of water, carbon dioxide, and ketones in cometary spectra. In the context of a Large-Scale Federated Learning Environment with highly diverse data, entities typically hold sensitive personal information and possess data that is greatly differing in nature, presenting a significant challenge for the training of accurate and unbiased models. To address this challenge, researchers have an emerging interest in multi-tenant horizontal federated learning, where entities with diverse data participate in a random walk to meet at a central hub for model training, without the need for centralized data management. This research fills an existing gap by introducing a novel algorithm, Random Walk Federated Learning (RWFL), tailored for entities with categorically heterogeneous data. RWFL uses a walk-based approach to concentrate learning on categories supported by multiple entities, thereby ignoring the information from a single source. Additionally, RWFL achieves a balance between the diversity of data and the level of precision in the model, by adapting the random walk's length in response to performance on a validation set. Experimental results, conducted across multiple, complex scenarios demonstrate the efficacy of RWFL, with this approach yielding model precision rates that are superior to those achieved through conventional federated learning methods. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2015 examined how a requirement for defendants to complete a mental health diversion program as part of their sentence affects their future mental health treatment-seeking behavior.  To achieve this, I utilized a difference-in-differences methodology, comparing three groups of defendants based on whether they were ordered to participate in a mental health diversion program, had the option to do so, or were not given this choice.  The data revealed that individuals required to participate in a diversion program were more likely to seek future mental health treatment.  This outcome held true for programs related to both felony and misdemeanor convictions.  Furthermore, I found no substantial differences in treatment-seeking behavior ten years after the diversion program was implemented.  The results also demonstrated that being ordered into a diversion program decreased suicide attempts and improved overall mental health, according to self-reported accounts.  Slightly varying estimates were obtained with different control variables, although the majority demonstrated a positive effect from the diversion programs.  Alternative specifications yielded estimates indicating a 25-30% increase in treatment-seeking behavior among those ordered into a diversion program compared to those who were not.  A simulation of missing data due to defendant death or parole noncompliance did not significantly impact the results.  A placebo test conducted during a period with incomplete data showed that the analyzed period's results were legitimate.  The findings suggested that requiring convicted individuals to participate in a mental health diversion program leads to an increase in future treatment-seeking behavior, implying that this approach could be an effective strategy for addressing mental health disorders within the criminal justice system. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new regularization technique, Consistency Regularization for Oversampled Data, which can be easily implemented to enhance the performance of semi-supervised image segmentation. This method leverages a simple consistent learning framework, combining oversampling and data augmentation techniques, to provide accurate predictions on underannotated images. Our proposed technique can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning models, and we demonstrate its versatility by successfully applying it to both transverse myelitis lesion segmentation and pancreatic tumor classification. Our findings, validated across multiple datasets, reveal substantial gains in model performance in low-annotation scenarios. Our proposed technique boasts a minimal computational footprint and requires no costly retraining, making it a versatile solution for a broad spectrum of real-world applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/CR-Oversampling.

To understand the progression of these dynamics and the role of interconnecting components, research focuses on the quantum version of the well-known Lotka-Volterra model. However, analyzing these complex interactions relies on rigorous mathematical simulations. In contrast, our approach involves training a graph neural network on a reduced model, incorporating only the basic elements and their connections, and we show that it's capable of replicating the dynamics of the intricate system. By applying a dimensionality reduction technique to the network's state, we gain insight into the dynamics, uncover hidden patterns, and determine the importance of each component's interaction. In the context of a highly chaotic system based on the Lotka-Volterra model, we demonstrate that by settling for a simpler paradigm that limits the system's complexity, we can identify the onset of chaos. Moreover, we show that by focusing on a local perspective and analyzing the dynamics of a small subset of components, we can predict the system's behavior on a larger scale. In the process, we discover that the emergence of chaotic dynamics in a small group of components can signal the onset of entropy in the entire system. Knowledge Tracing (KT) models leverage student interaction data to predict upcoming correct answers, and their effectiveness can be assessed using various metrics such as accuracy thirty days into the future, known as deep knowledge tracing's primary evaluation metric. Despite the simplicity of these models, their implementation has become complex due to the use of sophisticated neural network designs, different data representation methods, and diverse evaluation protocols. As a result, it has become a challenge to compare the performance of different KT models easily. This paper presents a Python-based platform, pyKT, that aims to streamline the evaluation of Knowledge Tracing models. pyKT addresses issues such as inconsistent data representation, varying future time frames, and uneven student selection for evaluation. The platform offers pre-trained models based on neural network-based Knowledge Tracing methods, allows users to upload their own models, and provides multiple evaluation protocols for research purposes. We evaluate pyKT using four distinct datasets and demonstrate that models trained on pyKT consistently outperform those trained without the platform on two of the four datasets. We also explore the importance of student filtering and future time frames in evaluation protocols and show that pyKT's default settings yield the best performance across all the datasets considered in this study. Notably, we discover a model that exceeds the 80% accuracy thirty days into the future on one particular dataset, a milestone considered challenging to achieve. We make pyKT available at https://pykt.org/.

The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates, where devices send graded updates to the server at their own pace without waiting for others to join. The flexibility of FedBuff enables a wide range of devices, including those with limited memory, to participate in learning without restriction, making it a highly efficient method for real-world applications. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unfamiliar environments.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to a real-world marine robot guidance problem.  Our code is available at https://github.com/sparse-gp/spgp-td.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a complex, anisotropic relativistic star composed of multiple components, effectively treating it as a dual-fluid object. By applying this approach, we derive specific equations that the star must satisfy and determine how they can be transformed into a dual-fluid model. This involves developing two key parameters that characterize the stress-energy properties of each fluid component and determining how they change across the star. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of fluid anisotropy on the star's structure and determine that it differs significantly from the results obtained using a standard multi-fluid model. By utilizing these findings, we are able to provide a new equation that describes the relationship between the pressure gradient and the Weyl tensor, primarily driven by the anisotropy of the stress-energy. This discovery holds importance for modeling self-gravitating rotating neutron stars composed of hadrons or solids, as well as neutron stars composed of quarks. It also extends the application of the semi-tetrad method beyond just static, rotating stars, by including barotropic stars that are rotating and oscillating. Additionally, we demonstrate that the semi-tetrad method provides a suitable framework for investigating stellar instability, specifically the anisotropic four-speed instability of a star, and the method's versatility allows it to be integrated with other physical phenomena, such as magnetic fields and charged matter, and with other mathematical formulations, including the F-2 method. It is noteworthy that the name "semi-tetrad method" is actually a misnomer, as this technique is best referred to as a "4-4 formalism" since it involves a 4x4 matrix. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper presents a novel approach to domain adaptation for GEC utilizing meta-learning. Specifically, it develops a method that leverages rich source domains to create a highly adaptable model, enabling seamless adaptation to a new target domain with just a limited amount of data. The proposed framework combines the benefits of meta-learning and maximum likelihood estimation to train models at both the source and target domains. Experiments conduct domain transfers using 5 different source domains with 5 target domains. The results show that the proposed method outperforms basic training and a baseline model incorporating pseudo data. Moreover, the proposed method achieves the highest score on the FCEC dataset among all domains, with a 0.39 average F score improvement over the baseline. Finally, analyzing the transfer learning process using a visual tool reveals that the model successfully adjusts to new data during the adaptation process. The code for this paper is available at github.com/ghrua/metagec.

The problem of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents within a cooperative game theory framework is a complex issue that has been explored by scholars for its implications on Pareto efficiency and fiscal fairness in tax collection and public service provision. However, most existing research assumes that agents' actions are non-strategic, which isn't a realistic assumption. In our study, we examine the distribution of indivisible goods among competitive and cooperative agents using combinatorial auction design. Our primary focus is on identifying pure Nash equilibria configurations that maximize fiscal fairness while ensuring the existence of cooperative solutions at each agent's marginal value. We introduce a new mechanism called the "Round-Robin Bundle Construction" method, which enables us to characterize the set of all pure Nash equilibria based on a key graph theory concept called a "matching." We also prove that this mechanism leads to cooperative solutions at the level of each individual agent's marginal value in a wide range of situations, although it does not result in fiscal fairness in general. On the other hand, we show that there is a specific scenario in which the "Rolling Textbook" method, known for ensuring fiscal fairness, contains a pure Nash equilibria where one agent is allocated an item at a cost greater than its value, demonstrating that it is not fair in that case. Our study builds upon our previous work and contributes a pure Nash equilibria configuration to the "Nash Equilibrium Tree" framework proposed by an unrelated research group. Moreover, we establish that the "Rolling Textbook" method can produce trees with the maximum possible number of leaves in a specific scenario, and discover a connection between the structure of these trees and the distribution of agents' values. A publicly available dataset is utilized to train and test the CNN, which demonstrates its potential for wide application in radiation treatment planning.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Scalar coding gain amounts to 1.5dB, with a 30% reduction in data transfer between base station and mobile terminal. Moreover, this approach facilitates seamless system entry, as the codebook is effectively 'learned' during initial measurement transmission. The proposed method's efficacy is consistently demonstrated across diverse scenarios.

A type of motion known as surface currents can be observed in two-dimensional lattices, where particles move along the edge of a lattice instead of throughout its entire structure. Researchers have achieved control over these currents by applying nonequilibrium conditions in one-dimensional situations. However, the construction of sturdy surface currents through interplay between nonequilibrium driving and geometric factors in three-dimensional lattices remains unexplored. This study demonstrates the feasibility of designing robust surface currents in three-dimensional Hofstadter models, independent of specific initial conditions. By matching nonequilibrium driving frequencies with geometric parameters of the lattice, leakage into the bulk can be prevented, and communities of particles that share the same renewal time can be identified, exhibiting distinct nonequilibrium behaviors. Further research on surface currents in three-dimensional lattices is facilitated by this study, with potential applications in the visualization of nonequilibrium dynamics, the identification of localization patterns, and the incorporation of surface currents into topological surface states. This approach is applicable to realistic situations, as it allows for the introduction of irregular shapes and anomalies in the lattice. This research was theoretically demonstrated, and suggestions for experimental verification have been provided. This work was finalized by outlining a prospective way to combine surface currents and topological states in three-dimensional lattices. Most massive stars end their lives. A significant portion dies in massive supernovae explosions, while the remainder collapses into massive compact objects like black holes or neutron stars. Research suggests that certain compact objects are likely paired with massive stars in binary systems. These binary pairs can result from massive stars that experienced a lesser explosion known as a thermonova, rather than a supernova. This study examines the constraints on the thermonova rate in the Galaxy based on the non-detection of thermonovae. It determines the overall thermonova rate in the Galaxy and identifies potential variables, finding that the key one is the time it takes for an star to lose a certain amount of mass. It also finds that this time must be longer than a million years. In the context of thermonova explosions, this time is crucial because it affects how often a star and a compact object in a binary system will separate far enough that the star can explode as a thermonova rather than a supernova. Therefore, this study calculates the minimum mass above which a star will always stay in binary with a compact object, the bondi mass loss rate that allows this minimum mass to be as low as 12 solar masses, or half its expected value. It further finds that this bondi mass loss rate must be less than a small fraction of its free-fall rate, which is the rate at which stars dissipate matter and collapse. Consequently, this study calculates the maximum allowed rate of mass loss for stars that will always remain in binary with a compact object, defining it as the bondi mass loss rate that is a tenth of a percent of their free-fall rate. It determines this maximum rate to be no more than 2.5 times 10 to the 4th power per solar mass per year. This rate is so low that it is unlikely to be relevant for the thermonova criterion in the Galaxy. However, it becomes important for masses greater than 25 solar masses. This study also examines the evidence for the bondi mass loss rate based on individual stars, finding that it is too scattered to be certain, but suspect that it may be influenced by external factors like metal content and stellar motion. It further finds that the bondi mass loss rate that allows this variation to be as large as 50 percent to be no more than 10 to the 4th power per solar mass per year. This rate is even lower than the previous rate, making it even more unlikely to be relevant for the thermonova criterion in the Galaxy

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. The development of our range control protocol, including non-uniform data restriction techniques, is also made available open source. The code can be used to create tools for CNN developers, helping them find suitable range control methods to detect and prevent hardware-induced errors in computer vision applications. The framework supports popular deep learning platforms like TensorFlow and PyTorch. The discovery of non-uniform techniques is also significant, providing an cost-effective way of preventing silent errors and memory malfunctions in limited-resource embedded systems. The results obtained can be compared to more complex and less efficient silence error detection methods like dropout and Bayesian neural networks. The reduction of silent errors and memory malfunctions in vehicle classification led to a decrease of 20% in accuracy and 30% in classification time, with an increase of 30% in computation required for range control. The increased demand for artificial intelligence in safety-critical applications is also discussed, along with the need for reliable and efficient CNN hardware, requiring reliable and efficient deep learning software. We introduce the first method to create a unified multi-lingual semantic space where similar words are represented by identical vectors regardless of the language in which they are expressed. Our approach, called CSE-CLUST, ensures that words with the same meaning are mapped to the same vector within the same cluster. We achieve this by forming non-overlapping clusters from multi-lingual word collections and then mapping words to the same vector if they belong to the same cluster. Our approach is efficient, simple, and effective as it utilizes existing multi-lingual semantic space pre-training techniques. We utilize the Google Translate API to collect 12 multi-lingual word collections, each consisting of 5 different languages. We establish that CSE-CLUST significantly outperforms the current multi-lingual semantic space pre-training techniques in multiple evaluation metrics. We also demonstrate that CSE-CLUST's cluster-consistent embedding feature allows it to accurately determine the language in which a given word is expressed. We further show that CSE-CLUST's representation can be utilized in multi-lingual classification and machine translation tasks, resulting in improved performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Multi-lingual-Word-Embedding.

Furthermore, our study reveals that the rates of (anti-)protons and phi mesons in these collisions are substantial enough to merit detailed experimental examination. Furthermore, our calculations indicated that the rates of these hadrons in xenon-nucleus collisions at midrapidity are directly proportional to the square of the collision energy, a relationship that we validated through our calculations. In late October 2019, violent demonstrations and widespread chaos broke out in Santiago, the capital of Chile, leading to over 300 reported fatalities and extensive property damage throughout the country's cities. This paper aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French subway car bombings to analyze the underlying dynamics of these events. The original model simulated area-level transmission rates based on local observations, but we've modified it to account for the geographical scope of the projections and the projections themselves. By applying this non-local epidemiological model to the unfolding protests, we were able to predict the rapid spread of violent unrest across Chile and the significant impact of governing authorities' responses on the protesters' overall behavior. The model's results are compared to actual event data, and we discuss the implications of these findings for both epidemiological models and the events that inspired them. The appendices include a discussion of the original model's calibration issues and an examination of the model's applicability to more general social dynamics. The data and code used in this study are available online. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the inclusion problem with regular expressions, taking into consideration variables representing unknown strings. These variables can be incorporated into the expressions by using union, concatenation, and star operations, as well as a new activity, specifically with variables. However, the method does not support negation over variables. Our algorithm initializes a decision tree based on the regular expression variables, without considering the string variables, which enables efficient solving of constraints by examining the tree node by node. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by incorporating the decision tree method into the Brzozowski regular expression abstract machine (MRE), and further show that this combination outperforms the existing approaches for both random-generated and real-world constraints. The method we developed is not limited to inclusion testing and can also decide whether one regular expression is equal to another, as well as determine the solvability of equation systems over regular expressions. The source code for the MRE solver is available online. The research also expands the set of regular expression constraints previously studied in the context of string constraints, and further contributes to the development of the Brzozowski regular expression abstract machine. The results we obtained can be improved, as shown in the evaluation results, which also outline the challenges remaining in the research. The evaluation was conducted at the Workshop on Regular Proof Theory, held in 2020. The rerefencing of the work done is requested in the form of the following reference: Esposito, L. et al. Mobile robots and autonomous systems require efficient and robust localization techniques to navigate their environments. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide accurate and real-time orientation and position information, but their state starts unknown and drifts over time. To address these challenges, we investigate deep learning models for visual-inertial localization, specifically using IMUs and a single camera, and propose the EMA-VIO framework with external memory attention. This model initially estimates the initial state and time-varying corruption term in the inertial measurements, and then incorporates a motion prediction module to enhance performance. Experimenting with an IMU setup and a 1080p camera, our results show that EMA-VIO outperforms traditional and learning-based methods in various scenarios, and the source code is available online at https://github.com/liyeyang/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, yet certain materials exhibit non-linear quantum behavior driven by symmetry, which could reach the point of no return with the introduction of a new class of materials, dubbed square-root topological materials. These materials possess unique properties, including a gap that vanishes when a two-dimensional surface is created, and a novel non-linear analog of the Weyl criterion that must be met. We propose a new topological material class, square-root higher-order Weyl materials, as a combination of square-root topological materials and higher-order Weyl materials, offering an exclusive non-linear endoskeleton that defines their 3D bulk non-linear phonons and 2D surface states simultaneously. We predict that these materials can be identified by means of non-linear monopole phonons in three dimensions and by a square-root form of the Fermi arc in two dimensions. Our theoretical findings can be applied to real-world materials based on atomic and molecular structures, and we propose potential experimental implementations utilizing photonic and acoustic systems. Our model also demonstrates that square-root topological materials can be synchronized with their surroundings, while maintaining their unique properties, making them an exciting area of study for condensed matter systems. We have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework that encompasses both square-root topological materials and higher-order Weyl materials, representing an innovative approach to describing non-linear topological phases in both bulk and surface states. Our work paves the way for exploring the complex interplay between square-root topological materials and their environment, and we have introduced the square-root Weyl semimetal phase that can be realized in both 3D and 2D configurations, along with a proposed experimental verification using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy. Our model represents a non-linear analog of the Weyl semimetal phase that can be described using a square-root form of the Fermi arc in two dimensions and a non-linear analog of the Weyl criterion in three dimensions.
