This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. This study builds upon prior research by extending its scope to time-dependent scenarios and presenting a detailed exploration of a more complex problem. It also examines the impact of different regularization techniques and time-dependent domain scenarios. The numerical solution method can be adapted for similar problems involving the Helmholtz equation. The software code used for these experiments is available online. This work is part of a broader project aimed at developing a real-time reconstruction technique for boundary data in the context of electromagnetic applications. Therefore, the findings and the numerical approach can be applied to similar problems involving the Helmholtz equation. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FSC) issue, a new problem that arises in interconnecting distributed knowledge bases, specifically in a federated setting. We envision a scenario where different entities, possessing independent data sources, want to combine their information by exchanging specific facts. Since these entities have closed systems, they cannot establish direct connections or share their raw data freely. As a result, they must maintain the solitude of their original data and maintain connectivity through secure, isolated connections. We propose a method to address FSC, a more complex problem that includes handling inference issues, as shown in our feasible solution approach. Additionally, we provide a precise framework for evaluating FSC solutions, capturing various aspects of such systems. This investigation was conducted as part of the efforts to develop an effective method to handle the FSC issue, although our primary contribution lies in identifying the problem and defining an evaluation framework for it. We believe that both achievements will benefit the community working on the Federated Learning Platform. We have demonstrated the practical application of our FSC issue in a prototype system called FedSelect, incorporating it into the open-source Hermitian reasoner as an example use case. FedSelect is distinct from other approaches as it allows for exchanging structured information as well as connecting different ontological models, offering the added benefit of validating the connectivity of the combined knowledge base. Notably, FedSelect has practical value beyond its designed purpose, showcasing that the issue we identified is more general and more widely applicable. We have tested FedSelect on extensive, real-world datasets, obtaining promising results and improving the existing methods. We have also explored various parameters of FedSelect, demonstrating its scalable and efficient performance in combining knowledge bases. We have further developed an automated approach to generate golden standards for validation, in addition to providing source code for FedSelect, Hermitian, and the evaluation framework, all available for public use. We have addressed the FSC issue in a centralized setting, which we believe has value on its own, given the limited research available on this topic. We analyze the effect of extending the rational numbers to quartic fields within the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$ on the rank of an elliptic curve. Previously established results for rank-increasing phenomena in quadratic and cubic extensions hold in specific cases of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions, respectively. Our research reveals additional instances within these two groups where a rank-increasing phenomenon occurs. Specifically, for the $A_4$ group, we find rank-increasing situations among curves with a specific 2-torsion subgroup structure. Moreover, among curves with a specific reduction behavior, we prove rank-increasing phenomena for the $S_4$ group. Our evidence suggests that the rank-increasing phenomenon may be common in $S_4$ quartic extensions. The proposed method of investigating rank-increasing phenomena involves examining subfields of the quartic extension and applying results on the rank of elliptic curves within quadratic extensions. The condition of having a specific reduction behavior can be viewed as a number-theoretic formulation of the 2-transitivity of the $A_4$ group, and it is achieved through combining the action of the Galois group and the action of the Weyl group $D_4$ on the isogenies defined by the quadratic subfields. The proposed method can be applied to other situations of $S_4$ and $A_4$ extensions. The proof of a rank-increasing phenomenon for a particular curve was previously established by Gross, using a different approach. The research was conducted as part of the editors' PhD work under the supervision of Ramakrishna. The paper is dedicated to his memory. The proposed method can be applied to show that the rank-increasing phenomenon may occur in the $S_4$ quartic extensions generated by the two independent algebraic points on the genus 3 curve defined by the net of G m /K3, although this result is yet to be confirmed. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to become indistinguishable from a target state, utilizing asymmetry monotonoes as metrics. Asymmetry monotonoes, which gauge the degree of directed classical or quantum non-equilibriumness, lead to speed limits on qubit systems, mapped onto the Euclidean hypersurface of the Bloch ball. By taking the maximum speed limit applicable to a system as its dynamics evolves, we find that it is directly related to the time it takes for two qubit states to become indistinguishable. Furthermore, asymmetry monotonoes yield distinct time intervals for comparing the distinguishability of a initial state with a set of target states, categorizing the states that can be distinguished from each other. We demonstrate that for initial and target states with equal overall population, the time it takes to become indistinguishable is proportional to the angle between their state vectors. Additionally, we find that initial and target states with equal overall population, and that are farthest from each other on the Bloch ball, require the maximum time to become indistinguishable, equivalent to half the time it takes to rotate 180 degrees around the equator of the Bloch ball. We map the time it takes for two qubit states to become indistinguishable onto the geometric structure of the Bloch ball, providing a simple and intuitive understanding of the concept. Furthermore, we show that the time it takes for a qubit state to become indistinguishable from a target state is directly related to the curvature of the hypersurface defined by the speed limit as it evolves in time. We demonstrate that the time it takes for two qubit states to become indistinguishable is an increasing function of the angle between their state vectors, and that it reaches a maximum when the initial and target states are directly opposite each other on the Bloch ball. We demonstrate that the time it takes for a qubit state to become indistinguishable from a target state is independent of the direction in which it rotates around the Bloch ball, but does depend on the radius of the circle defined by its evolution. If $H_K$ and $H_L$ are viewed as subspaces of a larger space equipped with the Hermitian form induced by $H_K$ and $H_L$, then the norm $\|T_N\|$ can be further bounded by $\sqrt{2}\cdot \kappa_{KL}^{1/2}$, where $\kappa_{KL}$ is the square of the ratio between the norms of the induced space and its subspaces. The minimal value of $\|T_N\|$ arises when $H_L$ is viewed as a subspace of $H_K$, resulting in the $\|T_N\|$ norm equaling $\sqrt{2}$. The paper also provides alternative expressions for the $\|T_N\|$ norm in the case of Hilbert spaces. The utility of these results is demonstrated through the examination of a specific operator inference problem. The paper's findings can be applied to both constant-based and variable-based assessments of the $\|T_N\|$ norm. The relationship between the $\|T_N\|$ norm and the underlying spaces' characteristics suggests that the $\|T_N\|$ norm is directly proportional to the square root of the space's Hermitian form induced norm. The paper's results provide valuable insights into the behavior and dynamics of the $\|T_N\|$ norm, which can be utilized in a variety of theoretical and applied settings. The results presented in the paper can be extended to other related contexts, such as multi-dimensional spaces and operator inference problems involving multiple operators. The paper's findings also highlighted the importance of considering the context in which the $\|T_N\|$ norm is assessed, which can significantly impact the resulting value. The results presented in the paper can be utilized in a variety of ways, including but not limited to the examination of operator inference problems, the analysis of Hilbert spaces, and the development of new techniques for assessing the $\|T_N\|$ norm. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This study highlights the potential of integrated quantum elements, combining both semiconductor and microwave engineering, and the value of terahertz near-field characterization in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is a contribution to the EUROVELENS project.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to evaluating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, focusing on the efficacy of our method in discovering the underlying structure of complex data. This involves assessing the accuracy of our approach in estimating the parameters and determining the number of excitable variables, along with a comprehensive evaluation of our method's performance in realistic scenarios. Our results show that this approach outperforms the existing literature in various scenarios and highlight the importance of inhibitory effects in shaping data and influencing model performance. We have also found that the introduction of random initial times affects the estimated parameters and duration of activity, and that our method is sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, which can be challenging to determine correctly. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely intense laser conditions. This component can modify the polarization of laser pulses with fluences reaching PW levels and enforces a specific spatial pattern on the electric field distribution, potentially interfering with waveplate efficiency. However, our simulations indicate that a thin, optimized waveplate can overcome this limitation by enhancing the pulse energy by a factor of 30 despite a limited impact on polarization alteration and spatial pattern formation. This discovery suggests that plasma waveplates could serve as a versatile tool in laser pulse polarization and spatial structure modification, offering a promising approach for defeating constraints posed by solid-state optics in high-power laser applications. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In contrast, a random error matrix can be corrected to a distance of n-k from the code, with probability tending towards 1 as the code length grows. This is achieved through a combination of our proposed decoding algorithm and the application of large numbers theory. In addition, we compare our decoding algorithm's performance to a previous method implemented on a random error matrix. Our analysis reveals that our proposed algorithm outperforms the existing method and, in some cases, exceeds twice the code distance of n-k when the code length grows infinitely. In our investigation, we also derive an expression for the probability of decoding a random error matrix of rank n-k, which can be seen as an extension of an earlier result presented by Khol'kin. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo's explosive energy and hydrogen envelope characteristics fall within the range of other SNe~II, implying that its distinct features arise primarily from the low mass range rather than unusual physics. Finally, we found that SN~2020jfo had a significantly higher absolute magnitude at the plateau endpoint compared to other SNe~II, which may indicate a precursor mass on the higher end of the range. Nonetheless, this paper's results are sensitive to the SN~2020jfo plateau duration estimation, which is subject to further adjustment. Moreover, further research is necessary to validate the 10 to the power 8 ergs per second explosive energy estimation. Lastly, SN~2020jfo's precursor mass requirements need more accurate modelling to be confirmed.

To investigate the impact of cosmic velocity field on dark matter halo mass function, we employed a deep learning approach with a generative adversarial network. By producing a range of cosmic velocity fields with specific characteristics, we created artificial N-body simulations of dark matter. These simulations allowed us to accurately determine the velocity effects on halo mass function, revealing a fundamental relationship that can be conveniently analyzed. Our analysis revealed the connection between velocity field and halo mass function through a modified Navarro-Viraldi density profile. In particular, we found that the velocity field influences the halo mass function primarily by affecting the characteristic density of halos, with a minimal impact on the slope of the halo mass function. Furthermore, our results demonstrated that the velocity field exceeds its own gravitational influence, which has a limited impact on the halo mass function. Furthermore, we discovered that the average velocity field within halos is directly proportional to their mass, with a characteristic density density ratio of 0.5. By incorporating the generated velocity field, we were able to accurately determine the halo mass function through a simple, closed-form expression, which can be applied to various velocity field scenarios. Our findings have implications for dark matter models and provide a precise, analytical method for predicting the halo mass function based on the velocity field, which can be useful for large N-body simulations. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations aimed to track changes in distribution and total mass over time, with the key prediction being that coherent patterns persist even after a marked change in conditions. 

These findings have been obtained through extensive supercomputing power, with up to 1024 cores used for a single simulation, and have resulted in a new code called "RelEvolution," its source code available online. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Moreover, our approach surpasses traditional supervised learning methods when the number of labeled data points is low, and even manages to rival the performance of fully annotated datasets once a certain threshold is reached. Our code is now available online for others to build upon.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We detail a deep learning platform developed in-house, entitled WaveNet, and highlight the challenges faced and potential improvements. Given the expected rate of detections for future LIGO-like detectors, we also explore methods to enhance the efficiency of this network in real-time applications. Ultimately, this deep learning framework has the potential to maximize the detection efficiency of neutron star and black hole binaries in real-time, across a wide range of signals, and on various detector platforms similar to LIGO. We conclude by examining the scope for enhancing WaveNet and integrating it with existing electromagnetic observation pipelines. Given its broad applicability, this network has the potential to contribute significantly to a broader range of research and applications, extending beyond its primary purpose of facilitating multi-messenger astronomy. We demonstrate this through the detection of spurious signals on advanced Virgo, revealing new information about the detector itself. Furthermore, we exhibit the capacity of WaveNet to enhance the understanding of dense matter by classifying neutron star binaries based on the mass ratio, a previously unexplored area. We also explore the potential of WaveNet to analyze binary black hole mergers, revealing interesting insights into the structure of these events. Given its innovative features and extensive capabilities, WaveNet offers a valuable solution for a wide range of research and applications in gravitational physics. To evaluate this hypothesis, we analyzed data from a large metropolitan area where traffic camera images were used to estimate the change in face-to-face encounters in public places between spring 2020 and spring 2021. After accounting for changes in public mobility, our findings showed that public encounters in urban areas decreased by about 50% in the first year of the pandemic and had not returned to normal levels by spring 2021. Furthermore, the reduction in encounters became more pronounced along socioeconomic lines, resulting in a more significant gap between high- and low-income diversity in the area studied. If similar trends continue in other areas, it could have far-reaching consequences for the income diversity of public spaces beyond just urban areas. The data used in this analysis are available online. The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on public space encounters in urban settings is an area that deserves further research, and we hope this study's results and data will help other scientists continue exploring this topic. The approach we used in this study could also be applied to other situations and locations, and we outline some possible examples in the paper. In this proof, a modified version of Stokes' formula for differential forms on a differential shaped manifold is demonstrated. To achieve this, the fundamental theorem for forms in a locally convex space is utilized as the underlying basis. This results in an alternative justification for the original Stokes' formula on a differential shaped manifold. Additionally, an expression for the divergence operator can be derived from this formulation. This approach also provides an explicit definition for the divergence operator when the metric tensor is non-degenerate. Furthermore, an integration by parts formula for differential forms as the immediate outcome of the modified Stokes' formula is demonstrated. This paper builds upon the previous work found in the paper titled "Integrating differential forms over a shaped space" by R. M. Hano, V. N. Tolpygin, and A. V. Tolpygin. A comprehensive examination of the requirements for the metric tensor to be non-degenerate or symmetric is also presented. This includes the discussion of the dual space and its corresponding metric tensor, as well as the integration of differential forms over a shaped space. A key aspect of this discussion is the analysis of the operator that transforms a differential form into its dual counterpart. This discussion eventually leads to the derivation of the modified Stokes' formula through the application of the fundamental theorem for forms in a locally convex space. This leads to the results presented in the original paper by Hano, Tolpygin, and Tolpygin. Therefore, this paper can be considered as the sequel to the mentioned previous work.

Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar territories poses a significant challenge for mobile robots, citing trade-offs between exploration and safety. To address this issue, we present an innovative sonar-integrated navigation system, tailored for mobile robots to navigate in dynamic, unknown environments. The system combines the sonar sensor's field-of-view expansion with the world model, enabling the robot to determine the sonar's effective field of view and prioritizing the sonar's scanning area to maximize exploration while ensuring the robot avoids collisions. The system's effectiveness was demonstrated in simulated and real-world settings, showcasing improved performance in uncertain environments and robust operation in the presence of moving obstacles. The results show that our system outperforms the conventional randomized approach in various evaluation metrics, including success rate, maximum score, and energy expenditure. The system's versatility was further highlighted in a landmark discovery task, achieving the highest score among the compared methods. The sonar-activated exploration path demonstrated a notable improvement in reducing energy expenditure in open environments. The system's code is available online at https://github.com/ali-gh/RTSC. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture, specifically the limitations of large-scale pre-trained language models like BERT, as well as opportunities for further innovation in the field of fake news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/AhmedHamdy1991/CMTR-BERT.

This research investigates the concept of a bending effect in Gaussian random fields, which refers to the presence of a sharp boundary beyond which no localized extremum can exist. We have achieved two primary goals in this study. Firstly, we have established a critical distance threshold, a square root of a variance component, below which no localized extremum can occur, provided the field's overall variance meets a specific criterion. Secondly, we have derived precise formulas to calculate the probabilities of no internal localized extrema existing within a specific distance range in a Gaussian random field. These probabilities can be determined using the inverse of the cumulative distribution function of the truncated standard normal distribution. We have further validated our results through numerical testing and compared them to existing models, in addition to analyzing various special cases. Furthermore, we have calculated the probabilities of no internal localized extrema existing within a specific distance range in two types of Gaussian random field models: one-type correlation field and fractal-like models. When analyzing data that contains a directionality property, standard principal component analysis (PCA) can be made more effective by implementing rotational invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA. This technique aims to find the rotation that minimizes the $\ell_1$-norm of the data matrix's eigenvalue-weighted sum. Unfortunately, this optimization problem lacks an efficient solution due to its non-smooth and non-convex nature. However, we present an iterative algorithm that yields a linearly convergent solution to this problem. We also introduce a specific application of rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA in machine learning, called robust PCA with the $\ell_1$-norm loss function. We then demonstrate that this algorithm produces an estimate that converges to the true answer at a rate of one only when the data matrix satisfies a certain moment condition. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to compare our algorithm with other baseline methods, showing that it outperforms them in terms of data recovery and classification accuracy. We have also openly released our code and an explanatory paper about the algorithm.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, as model size increases, their dependence on high-quality data has intensified, rendering annotation inefficiencies costly. This paper addresses this challenge in the domain of emotion-related question annotation. To enhance annotation efficiency, we introduced a two-stage process: initially, a limited amount of labeled data is used to train a semantic annotation model, which is then used to guide the annotation of new data by correcting user-provided partial labels. To ensure these partial labels are accurate, we developed a evaluation mechanism based on BERT. Ultimately, this paper presents findings from five participants who employed the proposed framework to annotate five different datasets, leading to a significant reduction in annotation time without compromising annotation quality. Furthermore, higher system performance was observed when these partially labeled data were used to train machine learning models, compared to standard supervised learning approaches. As such, the paper's contributions are twofold: it presents an economical annotation method that reduces time spent annotating data and an evaluation mechanism to ensure the quality of partially labeled data. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel navigation map concept consisting of two separate layers, designed to facilitate efficient mapping and path planning for robots operating in unknown environments. The topological map layer, combined with the global path planning algorithm Fast Marching Woods, enables the robot to determine a preliminary route by approximating the environment's perimeter. This approach allows the robot to establish a basic map without needing explicit location or distance measurements. In contrast to traditional mapping approaches, HiTMap reduces the need for extensive exploration in two key ways: by providing an initial map based on partial perimeter scans and by focusing exploration on filling in map gaps rather than creating an extensively detailed map. We have tested HiTMap on simulation models of office and museum environments and found it to be a highly efficient mapping system, outperforming existing methods in terms of exploration time while still generating highly accurate maps. Additionally, we have incorporated HiTMap into a hierarchical navigation system, which prioritizes the most critical decision-making tasks and reduces the load on the sensor module. This leads to a significant decrease in the number of measurements required, with the system we tested showing a 60% reduction in the number of required measurements in complex environments. We have also presented the design of HiTMap's control module, which includes a path correction module and a layer management module, and demonstrated its capabilities in a simulated airport scenario. We have made HiTMap's source code available online, inviting the mobile robotics community to contribute to and use this free, open-source mapping system. HiTMap's unique features make it suitable for a wide range of applications, including environmental monitoring, delivery robots, and search and rescue missions in unknown environments. In the future, we plan to explore the integration of HiTMap with other navigation systems, as well as the development of a localization module to transform HiTMap into a fully autonomous mapping and navigation system. We have also identified several challenges with the current version of HiTMap, including the occurrence of map loops, the inadequacy of the path planning algorithm for dense environments, and the limited range of the sensor module, and we propose potential solutions to these problems in our research. We believe that HiTMap's lightweight design and efficient mapping capabilities make it an ideal platform for integrating new features and navigating complex, dynamic environments. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This demonstrates the capability of atomic interferometry to detect the Meissner effect in various scenarios, including with certain materials that are difficult to interface with due to the required high sensitivity. This achievement also paves the way for using atomic interferometry to measure other subtle effects that are difficult to detect directly. The precision achieved can be further enhanced by increasing the atomic motion speed, which allows for the detection of the Meissner effect in materials with lower superconducting transition temperatures, as well as in nanoscale superconductors. This technique also offers a quantitative approach to measuring the expelled field's spatial distribution, adding a novel aspect to the measurement. The feasibility of this approach has been demonstrated by measuring the expelled field of a YBCO rectangle, showing that this method enables the non-destructive investigation of superconducting materials. This achievement opens up a range of applications, from evaluating superconductor interference pattern stabilities to analyzing the expelled field's role in atomic scattering, which can provide a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics. This technique can be implemented using available atomic interferometry systems and provides a promising solution for the various challenges faced in directly measuring the expelled magnetic fields of superconductors. We also show that positive weight mixtures equidistant from the origin are equivalent to models with constant weights. Furthermore, we analyze the concept of mixing distribution distances to the identity distribution, interpreting these distances as geometric measures that capture the diversity of the model's components. This framework's capabilities are demonstrated by applying these results to the analysis of mixture models, specifically in the study of mixing distributions equipped with a single parameter or two parameters, as well as in examining the distance between mixing distributions and the identity distribution, with distinct parameter values. We also discuss the implications of these findings for model selection and parameter estimation. Additionally, this study provides theoretical foundations that can be utilized to justify the use of specific mixing model criteria, such as the Integrated Complete Distance (ICD) metric, by proving that ICD is an appropriate measure of model fit. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging when using object-based programming models. This incompatibility exists because SIMD devices optimize best when executing large arrays of primitive data without explicit memory accesses by objects. In response to this limitation, researchers have developed various workarounds, such as rewriting codes using vector-based data structures, executing tasks on small batches, or combining object-based and vector programming in a hybrid approach. Despite these efforts, a fundamental aspect of object-based programming, namely dynamic memory allocation, has lacked efficient solutions. In response, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed to manage memory on SIMD devices and optimize for low overheads and efficient memory access patterns. Compared to existing, serial memory allocators, DynaSOAr reduces overhead by 2.5 times and outperforms a naive dynamic memory allocation approach by 1.5 times. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's simple and efficient design enables it to be easily integrated into existing object-based programming frameworks without the need for substantial code rewriting. In particular, we show that DynaSOAr can be used to improve performance in challenging applications like simulated object-based agents. In these simulations, DynaSOAr's hybrid memory allocation scheme proves particularly effective, resulting in a 20% performance improvement over a naive allocator and a 5% performance improvement over a state-of-the-art, serial allocator. In addition to its efficient memory allocation capabilities, DynaSOAr's design is versatile and can be easily adapted for use on other SIMD devices, including FPGAs. In contrast to FPGAs, however, DynaSOAr requires the presence of a fast host-memory interface to realize its full performance potential. In conclusion, DynaSOAr represents a significant advance in the development of parallel memory allocators for object-based programming on SIMD devices and provides a practical solution for addressing one of the key challenges associated with using such devices for general-purpose computing. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a single Mn atom bonded to a surface defect, a $d_{z^2}$-like YSR state was found to transform into a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like state once the separation from the defect increased to 4.5 nm. Moreover, in clusters, a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state reappeared as the spin polarization of adjacent Nb atoms became more localized. Experimental data was validated through theoretical calculations of magnetic moments in Mn clusters, revealing good agreement. However, due to limitations in accuracy, edge cluster atoms were not accurately modeled. A distinction was also drawn between aligned and detached adatoms in experiments, and possible pathways for edge cluster atom alignment discussed. A comparative study was conducted with Ti adatoms on Nb(110), revealing distinct differences in YSR states induced by the higher lying $3d^2$ Ti$^{2+}$ state due to its stronger coupling with the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ YSR state and the superconducting gap. Furthermore, in Mn clusters, multiple $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR states appeared as the separation between adatoms increased to 0.5 nm, a result that could be verified through experimental means. A proposed alignment of cluster atom spins, supported by magnetic force microscopy images, was also discovered. In conclusion, this theoretical framework has demonstrated its effectiveness in predicting the YSR states of magnetic impurities on a superconducting surface, and its applications in understanding YSR states in clusters and the effects of edge cluster atom alignment. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from $500$ to $700$ million years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie inside it, and further research into the stellar activity levels found moderate to high activity. Therefore, any possible habitability of TOI-712 d might be compromised. In a new finding, the team discovered that TOI-712 is actually a binary star system composed of two stars orbiting each other every $51.7$ days, with a mass ratio of about $0.5$. This discovery also revealed that TOI-712 is likely a young star with a mass similar to that of the Sun and a radius $60\%$ of the Sun's radius. In a historical discovery, the team found that TOI-712 was detected in a survey called the $All Sky Automated Survey$ using a $6.2$ magnitute filter, under the name VHS 06. To confirm the planetary nature of TOI-712.05, the team observed the star's orbital phase, which showed a deep partial transit. This confirmed that TOI-712.05 is a rocky world with a radius of $1.4$ times that of Earth. Concluding, TOI-712 is a young binary star hosting a system of four planets, including a rocky Earth-sized planet and a mini-Neptune-sized planet in the habitable zone. Although TOI-712 d shows signs of having a substantial atmosphere and geologic activity, it's uncertain if it's capable of supporting life due to the star's moderate to high activity levels. This letter proposes a strategy for detecting top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider through elastic proton-proton scattering. By searching for a clear signature of high-transverse-momentum same-sign leptons in events with zero net rapidity, the elastic production of top-quark pairs can be extracted from background processes. Using existing data, we demonstrate that the elastic production of top-quark pairs can be identified and measured with high precision. Furthermore, as the cross-sectional area for elastic scattering is significantly smaller than that for inelastic scattering, this method is inherently resistant to systematic uncertainties associated with luminosity estimation, which could also be applicable to future colliders such as the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider and the Future Circular Collider. We estimate that with the current 137-petabarn inverse bunch of data at the Large Hadron Collider, the top-quark pair production cross-section for high-transverse-momentum events can be determined with a precision of at least 13 percent, and this precision could be further improved to 7 percent with additional data collected at an energy of 13 TeV. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting individual top quarks rather than pairs, which would require more sophisticated analytical tools and possibly more data, but remains a viable possibility nonetheless. The precision with which we can determine the top-quark pair production cross-section for the Large Hadron Collider, as well as the discovery potential for the Future Circular Collider at energy levels of 13 TeV and 50 TeV, are estimated in tables that accompany this letter. The proposed analysis technique could be implemented using existing data processing frameworks, which are designed to search for top-quark pair production, but with a few key modifications to account for the distinct characteristics of elastic events. The large size of these frameworks can result in analysis computation times of several weeks on high-performance computers for a single data batch, which further complicates the calculation for larger datasets. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, a phenomenon supported by core mass function data.  Furthermore, the mean mass of protostellar cores exceeds the mean mass of the surrounding gas and dust within a 2.5 parsec radius by a factor of approximately 10.  This significant mass difference suggests that it takes significantly more mass to form a massive star than is commonly assumed, based on stellar mass distributions and the mass function of the Dragon core sample.  This conclusion is consistent with recent findings from other clouds, and it has implications for the core collapse and star formation efficiency, particularly in dense infrared dark clouds.  Finally, this research reveals that massive star formation likely originates from high-density cores with masses similar to those found in the Dragon cloud, rather than in less dense cores with lower mass limits set by magnetic support.  These findings also highlight the importance of distinguishing between protostellar and starless cores in defining the core mass function, as it affects the predicted mass range for newly formed stars. The steady-state behavior of a fluid interface subject to an advancing front in a Hele-Shaw cell with constant rotation rate is examined. Contrary to previous research which focuses on the development of a fingering interface or a stationary interface, we consider the effect of a rapidly moving reference frame due to rotation on a fluid interface in a Hele-Shaw cell. In this study, we take a variable curvature approach that enables the application of the rotating frame of reference concept. By doing so, we identify the key factor influencing the stability of a fluid interface as the rate of rotation squared divided by the curvature of the interface. This prediction can be confirmed through direct numerical simulation of a specific scenario in which a rectangular wedge of fluid is slowly inserted into a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. Additionally, we find that the rate of rotation squared divided by the curvature of the interface serves as a stability criterion in scenarios where the curvature of the interface changes over time. This is demonstrated in two cases: the instability of a planar interface subject to a constant shear stress, and the instability of a circular interface with a constant and gradual increase in radius. Furthermore, we examine the effect of the rate of rotation on the development of a fingering interface subject to an advancing front in a Hele-Shaw cell. In this case, we develop a nonlinear integral equation that enables the calculation of the stability of the interface for any rate of rotation. Based on this analysis, we find that the rate of rotation squared divided by the curvature of the interface serves as a linear function of the distance from the point of instability in the case of a rectangular wedge of fluid. In the case of a circular interface, we find that the rate of rotation remains constant as the radius of the interface increases, which indicates the development of a hyperbolic tangent-shaped interface. In both cases, we observe that the rate of rotation influences the distance from the point of instability rather than the shape of the interface. In the case of a planar interface subject to a constant and gradual increase in radius, we find that the rate of rotation determines the shape of the interface from a cusp-shaped interface to a fingering interface via a range of intermediate shapes. In the case of a circular interface subject to a constant and gradual increase in radius, we find that the rate of rotation determines the radius of the interface rather than its shape. In both cases, we demonstrate that the rate of rotation serves as a linear function of the distance from the point of instability or the radius of the interface, respectively.

In neural machine translation, generating text can be viewed as a sequential process, similar to searching a tree of possible phrases to convey meaning. This analogy inspires the introduction of a new mechanism, "look-ahead focus", which allows for the inclusion of additional context beyond the typical source sentence. This focus context is on the left side of the source sentence and represents the target phrase that has not been translated yet. By incorporating this feature, a neural network model is able to prioritize certain phrases over others, leading to more coherent and less fragmented translations. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms standard neural machine translation models in various evaluation metrics. Moreover, this model's performance can be further enhanced when combined with conventional methods, such as round-trip reinforcement learning, without significant computational costs. The associated code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-focus.

This work also highlights the value of a transformational development approach for refining existing technologies and the benefits of reusing astronomical research data, a vast and underutilized resource. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions is challenging due to the absence of suitable golden standards. In this research, a novel evaluation framework is presented that differentiates between gold-standard diagnoses derived from cell populations and individual cells. Specifically, it uses a two-part approach to assess nucleus segmentation: firstly, a comparison with general accuracy metrics is conducted to validate the quality of the segmentation on a large scale; secondly, a comparative analysis of individual cells is performed to validate the accuracy of the segmentation at the level of a single cell. This evaluation method, combined with an innovative nucleus segmentation dataset, enables accurate evaluation of nucleus segmentation protocols and algorithms. The proposed framework, alongside the provided dataset, has significant potential applications in cognitive computational learning and nucleus segmentation protocol optimization through reinforcement learning. The research was conducted in collaboration with pathologists and cancer patients and employs a straightforward and robust W-Net convolutional network protocol that can be readily utilized by other researchers in the field. The proposed framework and dataset have been utilized to demonstrate the effectiveness of U-Net, Fed-Net, and W-Net in nucleus segmentation tasks. This study expands on previous work by establishing the local exchange property for specific groups, namely the special orthogonal groups defined over a finite field with an odd number of variables and the symplectic groups defined over a finite field with an even number of variables. Moreover, it demonstrates that the local exchange property is inherent to these groups, without relying on specific characteristics. Consequently, this result implies that these groups possess a particular structural characteristic known as exchangeability. This study also examines the relationship between the characteristic of a field and the property of exchangeability, revealing that there are infinite sets of exchangeable groups within the families of the special orthogonal and symplectic groups. Finally, it demonstrates that the group $O_{2n+1}(2)$ is uniquely structured and cannot be exchangeable, whereas the group $Sp_{2n}(2)$ may or may not be exchangeable, depending on the value of $n$. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement along the direction of sound waves, which can be challenged by significant lateral shifts exceeding half a wavelength. This study introduces the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method to enhance lateral shift estimation in elastography. The VSSA approach aggregates sub-wavelength shifts in the spatial domain, enabling the estimation of mechanical properties even in areas with substantial lateral displacement. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, the VSSA algorithm showed significant improvements in estimation accuracy in simulations and experiments, with a particular advantage in imaging smaller structures. The results demonstrate the VSSA's potential for broad applications in elastography. The code associated with this study is available online at: https://github.com/alishere/VSSA. These games, set on a grid divided into distinct regions, require one player (the evader) to navigate away from the other (the pursuer) to a safety state defined within a specific region, while the pursuer aims to prevent this outcome. To achieve this, we propose a hierarchical decomposition of the grid, consisting of a high-level representation and a series of increasingly detailed sub-grids. This decomposition serves as the basis for a strategy profile consisting of simple rules for each sub-grid and a hierarchical approach to resolve conflicts. To facilitate this decomposition, we establish a characterizing equation for the set of safe states within each sub-grid, providing a starting point for its development. To illustrate the potential of this approach, we apply it to a sample grid, demonstrating the feasibility of hierarchical divisions in evader-evasion games. The Efficient Vector Boson Approximation (EVBA) method, previously validated in the context of electron-proton collisions, has been successfully applied to vector boson production in proton-proton collisions and beyond, including at high-energy muon colliders. Compared to the exact matrix element calculation, EVBA demonstrates significant speed improvements while maintaining accurate results, particularly in regions where the dominant contribution comes from weak-boson exchange. Evaluations conducted for $W$ and $Z$ production, with additional processes such as $WW$, $ZZ$, and heavy vector boson production, reveal that EVBA yields comparable outcomes to the exact method for observables that are highly sensitive to the weak interaction. Nonetheless, in the case of $W$ or $Z$ production at higher energies, slight discrepancies in certain observables are observable. To utilize EVBA in muon colliders, special consideration must be given to neutrino contamination, particularly for the $Z$ channel at lower energy facilities. To counter this, EVBA can be paired with optimised cuts that eliminate affected events, thereby restoring accuracy. To facilitate seamless integration with existing codes, the EVBA method has been implemented within the Amcgal event generator. Further optimization of the EVBA code is advised to enhance its performance for more complex processes. Nonetheless, in its present form, EVBA demonstrates that efficient weak-boson approximation remains a viable option for the study of physical processes at muon colliders. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to catastrophic forgetting of initial tasks as new ones are
introduced. To overcome this, we show that isolating sub-networks of the dynamics model significantly increases the effectiveness of multi-task reinforcement learning, allowing for a rich exchange of knowledge between tasks without a significant decrease in performance. We validate our approach against both simple and complex multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, employing both randomized and intentionally designed tasks. Our method, capable of destroying task isolation and enabling knowledge sharing, is dubbed Network Augmentation for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (NAMTRL). Our research highlights the potential of NAMTRL to improve multi-task reinforcement learning through the exchange of knowledge facilitated by dynamic neural networks. The three-balls conjecture for harmonic functions holds true without any restriction on the number of balls. In contrast, the three-balls conjecture for eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator was resolved by Siciek, while also being true for functions related to the Laplace operator with n distinct balls. Nonetheless, researchers such as Havin and Shapiro were unable to extend the three-balls conjecture to harmonic functions associated with the Dirac operator within Clifford analysis to more than two balls. In our present study, we successfully demonstrate the three-balls conjecture's validity for harmonic functions associated with the Dirac operator within Clifford analysis. The proposed approach also enables us to generalize the three-balls conjecture to be applicable for up to n balls, where each ball has a distinct radius. The proposed method, in particular, involves developing a non-degenerate operator based on the concept of radial Riesz decomposition, as well as establishing the uniqueness of this operator's solution. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing the posterior distribution of all possible images. We argue that evaluating the posterior distribution is more important than generating a single ideal solution, and focus on estimating the posterior distribution rather than finding a single representative sample from it. We propose a new algorithm, called Regularized Conditional GAN, that uses a regularized conditional GAN as the basic building block, and incorporates two key components: a quality measure to filter generated samples and ensure diversity, and a penalty term to prevent the generator from overfitting. We demonstrate that using a diversity-filtered set of conditional samples as input to the generator results in a Regularized Conditional GAN with filtered diversity, which is equivalent to a standard GAN with an additional term in the loss function. We further show that this is similar to a regularized version of the conditional inference problem, which can be solved using a gradient descent algorithm. We test this algorithm on low-light image enhancement and MRI image reconstruction, and the results show an improvement over existing methods. We measure the quality of the generated samples using two metrics: the frequency of valid samples as reported by the success rate of the algorithm, and the distance between real and generated samples as reported by the mean squared error. We recommend using a simpler evaluation method that focuses on estimating the posterior distribution rather than finding a single ideal solution, which can be achieved by measuring the frequency of valid samples as reported by the success rate of the algorithm. The interstellar medium is home to many regions with distinct properties, and mapping these regions is a major goal for investigating the physical environment through which pulses from pulsars travel to reach Earth. By examining pulse phase measurements from the radio telescope array of the Westbury long baseline array, researchers identified variations in delay and curvature, likely caused by scintillation of the pulsar B1133+16, which occurred between 2005 and 2011. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through an innovative pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing a deeply cascaded autoregressive architecture, yet its limited pitch control results from converted learned features instead of direct pitch signals being incorporated. To address this constraint, we propose a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional network where each stage draws from a combination of general and task-specific models. General models are shared across stages and facilitate global waveform understanding, while task-specific models are stage-independent and allow for local waveform analysis. The proposed network allows for direct incorporation of pitch signals through vector concatenation, thereby enhancing the limited pitch control of WN. Experimental evaluations on the LJSpeech and VCTK datasets demonstrate the improved pitch control of QPNet compared to WN, along with the potential for further performance enhancement when combined with other techniques such as multi-task learning. Code availability: https://github.com/Parandoss69/QPNet.

Our primary goal in this research is to demonstrate the challenging nature of a visual noise localization task, which can be achieved by various deep learning approaches but presents difficulties for traditional computer vision methods. To illustrate the hardness of this task, we create a challenging dataset featuring complex visual noises that surround a central character and demand sophisticated object-aware masking techniques to accurately define regions of interest. To further complicate the task, we introduce multiple diverse character masks that are modeled after various psychological theories and incorporate essential features of the surrounding environment. These masks also enable us to thoroughly assess the various object-aware masking techniques and related research by evaluating how different methods perform in response to varying levels of noise and distinct character masks. Our rigorous experiments involve incorporating a wide range of deep learning techniques that incorporate object-aware masking, including explicit masks created using segmentation networks and implicit masks derived from attention-based structures. Our findings show that despite the diversity of these techniques, many of them struggle with noisy character masks and demonstrate significantly inferior performance when compared to the conventional approach of focusing on the center of the image. Our research on the challenges of visual noise localization also involves delving into related psychological theories, providing a deeper understanding of the complex mechanisms that underpin object-aware attention and suggesting various future research directions in this area. Our challenging character noise dataset, complete with rigorous evaluation protocols, is made available to the public domain for the purposes of further development and testing of various object-aware masking techniques. Our ultimate goal in creating this research is to encourage other scientists to take up the challenging task of visual noise localization.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex interactions and relationships between entities in multi-agent scenarios, including areas like social network analysis and chemical compound study. However, a significant issue these networks encounter is the limited scalability to a large number of nodes, largely due to the widespread use of local graph representations. In response to this challenge, a novel framework called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN) is proposed, which leverages Lorentzian geometry to define a global framework incorporating a central node that represents the entire graph, thereby significantly expanding the network's scope while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, LGNN achieves a superior classification performance compared to conventional GNNs, while demonstrating a notable increase in model complexity. To validate our findings, LGNN is applied to multiple benchmark datasets, yielding notable improvements in classification accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate LGNN's versatility by applying it to a novel task called ring structure prediction in organic compounds, where it achieves a high precision of 86.34%. Our research introduces a innovative direction for GNNs that can handle large-scale datasets, and provides a cutting-edge approach to predict compound structures. Our LGNN code is available at https://github.com/Cheng28/Lorentzian-GNN.

This research focuses on a mathematical problem known as an inverse problem, where we aim to determine a sound wave source's characteristics within a complex structure that contains cavities, based on measurements taken from the surface of the structure. This task is challenging due to the limited information obtained from the measurements and the intricate relationship between the sound wave and the structure it generates. Sound waves can become distorted as they travel through a structure and may be affected by factors like the speed sound waves move at and the properties of the material they move through. As a result, identifying the source of a sound wave in a real-world scenario is extremely difficult and typically requires additional information about the structure and its properties. In this study, we develop an algorithm to determine the speed sound waves move at and the properties of the material they move through within a structure, which is then used to determine the sound wave source's characteristics. We test and evaluate our method using numerical data and real data obtained from a concrete cube with a built-in cavity. The algorithm works by breaking down the problem into smaller components, using a technique called the singular value decomposition, and creating a realistic sound wave source based on the measurements and the structure, which is then compared to the actual data and the structure it was generated from. The evaluation suggests that the algorithm works best when the sound wave source is concentrated in one area and there is little distortion in the sound wave.
